titel: Herrera: The Battle, and a Song of Victory
quelle: Fernando de Herrera, Relación de la guerra de Cipre y suceso de la batalla naval de Lepanto (Seville: Alonso Picardo, 1572, as the 1852 reprint gives the imprint; the Biblioteca Nacional records Alonso Escribano), chapters XXIV–XXVIII and the Canción, as reprinted in Colección de documentos inéditos para la historia de España, vol. XXI (Madrid, 1852), pp. 344–382; Internet Archive coleccindedocu21madruoft (University of Toronto).
hinweis: The Spanish voice of the battle, by one of the leading Spanish poets of the generation before Cervantes, who was not there. Herrera wrote in Seville within a year, from reports, letters and Italian printed accounts, and says so; where his sources disagree he argues, above all for Don John's share of the credit against the Venetians. The text is that of the 1852 reprint, which keeps Herrera's spelling but adds modern accents; the OCR is corrected by reading and checked against the page images. The copy of the 1572 print in the Biblioteca Nacional (R/3794) is digitised by the Biblioteca Virtual Miguel de Cervantes. The lists of galleys and captains and some passages of praise are shortened and marked […]. The English is this site's working translation (CC0); the song is translated in prose. Critical modern editions exist (Cátedra, 2022) and were not used.

sections.titel: Chapter XXIV: The two fleets seek each other
sections.blurb: The League's council on whether to turn back, Herrera's quarrel with the Venetian Quirini over whose resolution it was to seek battle, Kara Hoca's count of the League, and the Ottoman fleet coming out of the gulf.

units.orig: Dejando la Chafalonía la armada cristiana, aunque el viento no la consentía navegar, siendo necesario que fuese muy favorable ó á lo menos calma, porque convenía ir con grande orden, pues se hallaban ya tan cerca los enemigos. A seis de otubre sábado en la primera guardia se levó y navegó toda la noche al remo, por ser el tiempo contrario, aunque no forzoso, con intención de acercarse á los castillos de Lepante, porque el Barbarigo pedia que se entrase en el golfo, suplicando á D. Juan que no perdiese aquella ocasión, porque confiriendo últimamente en consejo por la dificultad de la empresa, que hacian lo que fuese mas provechoso, según dicen algunos, Juan Andrea y Ascanio y otros de la consulta eran de parecer que por la brevedad del tiempo y estar en tierra enemiga y haber de atravesar para volver á invernar el golfo de Venecia y costear la Pulla y Calabria, pues habian metido al enemigo en sus tierras huyendo, que desde allí se volviesen.
units.en: The Christian fleet left Cephalonia, although the wind would not let it sail, for it needed a very favourable wind or at least a calm, since it had to go in good order with the enemy so near. On Saturday 6 October, in the first watch, it weighed and rowed all night, the weather being contrary though not violent, meaning to approach the castles of Lepanto; for Barbarigo asked that they enter the gulf and begged Don John not to lose that opportunity. When the difficulty of the enterprise had lately been discussed in council, some say, to do what was most profitable, Gian Andrea [Doria], Ascanio [della Corgna] and others of the council were of the opinion that, since little time was left, since they were in enemy country and would have to cross the gulf of Venice and coast along Apulia and Calabria to go back to winter quarters, and since they had driven the enemy fleeing into his own lands, they should turn back from there.
units.titel: Turn back, or seek the enemy?
units.note: Herrera, a poet of Seville, wrote from the reports and letters that reached Spain and from Italian printed accounts, among them Contarini's (Contarini Battle [1]). He names those who counselled caution on the League's side too; compare Mehmed Bey in the Ottoman council (Contarini Council [13]).

units.orig: Don Juan y el Colona y el marqués de Santa Cruz con el Barbarigo que eran de opinion contraria, fueron de voto que se buscase la armada enemiga, y le representasen la batalla en la boca del golfo, y si saliese, pelearían, y sino allí diria el tiempo lo que debian hacer, ó se volverían habiendo ganado tanta reputación y nombre; pero el proveedor Quirino escribió que después de muchas consultas se hizo lo que él propuso siempre, que era ir á Petalá, puerto apartado del dicho golfo cuarenta millas, y de allí pasar á presentalle la batalla, y cuando el Bajá no quisiese salir, reconociendo los castillos si se podian ganar y entrar dentro, y cuando viesen que no queria salir á la batalla, lo tuviesen allí cerrado ó se pusiesen en otra empresa que lo obligase á salir contra su armada por defender sus lugares. Y así él, á sí solo atribuye esta honra. ¡Tan dulce es el nombre de la gloria y el deseo de la inmortalidad de la memoria en las cosas humanas, que aun se usurpan los hombres el merecimiento ageno! No niego yo que el Quirino, varón tan grave y que no queria engañar la universal fama, no fuese parte en este voto; pero no afirmo que fuese suya esta resolución, que solo se debe al valor de D. Juan de Austria por general confesión de todos, porque él con ánimo imitador de las hazañas de su padre y con dichosa y considerada determinación, comparando las fuerzas de ambas partes, se dispuso á la batalla y movió á su parecer á muchos; y así por inspiración divina mas que por alguna razón de la diciplina de mar, aunque era noche y cerca del enemigo y con viento contrario para buscallo, hizo dar señal de levar y partió, en lo cual consistió toda la salud dellos.
units.en: Don John, Colonna and the Marquis of Santa Cruz, with Barbarigo, who were of the contrary opinion, voted that they should seek out the enemy fleet and offer it battle at the mouth of the gulf; if it came out, they would fight, and if not, time would tell them there what to do, or they would go back having won so much reputation and name. But the provveditore Quirini wrote that after many councils what he had always proposed was done: to go to Petalá, a harbour forty miles from the gulf, and from there go and offer battle; and if the Pasha would not come out, to reconnoitre the castles and see whether they could be taken and the gulf entered; and when they saw he would not come out to fight, to keep him shut in there, or to take up some other enterprise that would force him to come out against their fleet to defend his places. And so he attributes this honour to himself alone. So sweet is the name of glory and the desire for an immortal memory in human affairs that men will even usurp another's merit! I do not deny that Quirini, so grave a man, who would not wish to deceive the common report, had a part in this vote; but I do not affirm that the resolution was his. It is owed only to the valour of Don John of Austria, by the general admission of all; for he, with a spirit that imitated his father's deeds and with a happy and considered resolution, comparing the forces of both sides, set himself to battle and brought many round to his opinion. And so, by divine inspiration more than by any reason of the discipline of the sea, although it was night, the enemy near and the wind against him for seeking him out, he had the signal given to weigh, and set out; and in this lay their whole salvation.
units.note: A Spanish author correcting a Venetian claim: Herrera's quarrel over credit is itself part of the League's story of rivalry (Liga Faith [5]). Contarini gives the credit to Don John 'encouraged by the exhortations of Agostino Barbarigo' (Contarini Battle [1]).

units.orig: Porque el Bajá tenia esperanza firme de encerrallos en el canal de la Chafalonía ó tomar la armada sobre el Ferro, porque Caracosa, alcaide de la Belona y famoso cosario, por el mucho conocimiento que tenia de la navegación y por la singular osadía de su ánimo se ofreció á ir con un batel y reconocer y contar la armada, y en hábito según dicen de pescador, llegó á la Gomeniza con tanta destreza, que no recibió embarazo ni impedimento alguno. Es verdad que por la priesa y el temor que podia tener, si era conocido, ó porque las demás galeras estaban tan apartadas que no pudo alcanzallas con la vista, no tomó entero el número de todas, y así pudo contar ciento y setenta, y volviendo muy alegre persuadió al Bajá, que siguiese la fortuna favorable de Selin que le daba en las manos aquella rica armada, donde iba entregada á la muerte toda la flor de la cristiandad: que no perdiese aquella ocasión, con que se hacia su Príncipe señor del resto de Europa, pues siendo los cristianos tan inferiores no podian dejar de perderse sin hacer alguna defensa. Y así siéndoles el viento maestro favorable con grandísima alegría se pusieron todos en orden, porque nunca temieron otro suceso sino la huida de los cristianos, trayendo para confirmación desto sus muchas vitorias y el grande número de galeras que traian, y según después se entendió de los cativos, referian que siendo ellos tan pocos en la Prevesa, que fué la jornada que mas daño hizo á la cristiandad, les huyó la armada de la liga, y que retirándose de Malta no perdieron algunas galeras, que como ellos decian vanamente, no les osaron ganar alguna escuadra dellas, como si fuera posible que D. García de Toledo con aquella pequeña armada pudiera acometer á tanta multitud de bajeles, no queriendo mas impía que justamente romper los venecianos las paces con Solimano, y acudir á la causa pública en defensa de la religión cristiana, con cuyo socorro no volvería su armada á Constantinopla.
units.en: For the Pasha had a firm hope of shutting them in the channel of Cephalonia or taking the fleet off the Ferro; because Kara Hoca, governor of Valona and a famous corsair, from his great knowledge of navigation and the singular boldness of his spirit, offered to go in a boat and reconnoitre and count the fleet, and, dressed, they say, as a fisherman, reached Gomenizza so skilfully that he met no hindrance or obstacle at all. It is true that, from haste and the fear he may have had of being recognised, or because the other galleys were so far off that he could not reach them with his eyes, he did not take the full number of them all, and so could count a hundred and seventy; and returning very cheerful he persuaded the Pasha to follow the favourable fortune of Selim, which was putting into his hands that rich fleet, in which the whole flower of Christendom was delivered to death: not to lose that opportunity, by which his Prince would become master of the rest of Europe, since the Christians, being so inferior, could not fail to be lost without making any defence. And so, the north-west wind being favourable to them, they all put themselves in order with the greatest joy, for they never feared any outcome but the flight of the Christians, bringing in confirmation their many victories and the great number of galleys they had; and, as was learned afterwards from the captives, they said that at Preveza, when they were so few, which was the day that did Christendom most harm, the League's fleet had fled from them; and that when they withdrew from Malta they lost no galleys, for, as they vainly said, no squadron dared attack them; as if Don García de Toledo with that small fleet could have attacked such a multitude of ships, the Venetians being unwilling, more impiously than justly, to break their peace with Suleiman and come to the common cause in defence of the Christian religion, with whose help his fleet would never have gone back to Constantinople.
units.note: Contarini gives Kara Hoca's count as a hundred and fifty (Contarini Council [2]); Herrera as a hundred and seventy. 'Retiring from Malta': the Ottoman withdrawal after the failed siege of 1565, when Don García de Toledo's relief fleet did not attack it.

units.orig: Con esta confianza los turcos gastaron todos aquellos dias en mucho placer por la grande presa que esperaban, y no querían dormir ni descansar sin que los ruegos de sus capitanes pudiesen con ellos, antes pasaban la noche cantando y tratando de la vitoria que les ofrecian sus enemigos mesmos, porque de cualquiera otra cosa hacian mas cuenta que de la milicia cristiana. Y en aquella noche mesma surgió su armada fuera de los castillos que están en las estrechuras del golfo de Lepanto, do aquel golfo ciñe tanto las bocas del mar Jonio que por menos de un estadio dista Etolia de la Morea, que por donde se cortan Europa y Asia por el Elesponto ó brazo de San George. En estas estrechuras, como es dicho, están los dos castillos Dardanelos de antiguo edificio, el uno en Acaya, llamado Rhio, y Molicreo en Etolia; pero este es mucho mas fuerte que el otro, porque Bayaceto, bisabuelo deste Selin, le añadió una gran torre y lo cercó de doblado muro. A la mañana enderezó el Bajá resoluto de venir en la vuelta de la armada cristiana, llevando docientas y treinta galeras reales, muchas dellas de veinte y ocho y treinta bancos, y setenta galeotas de veinte y veinte y dos bancos, sin otros bajeles, y con tanta gente que, con la ordinaria, y la que reforzó la armada y todo el resto, la gente que se halla en semejante empresa, pasaban de ciento y veinte mil.
units.en: In this confidence the Turks spent all those days in great pleasure over the great prize they expected, and would neither sleep nor rest, whatever their captains begged of them, but passed the night singing and talking of the victory their enemies themselves were offering them; for they took more account of anything else than of the Christian soldiery. And that same night their fleet anchored outside the castles that stand in the narrows of the gulf of Lepanto, where that gulf so pinches the mouths of the Ionian Sea that Aetolia is less than a stadium from the Morea, [narrower] than where Europe and Asia are cut apart by the Hellespont or arm of Saint George. In these narrows, as has been said, stand the two castles called the Dardanelles, of ancient building, the one in Achaea, called Rhion, and Molycrion in Aetolia; but this one is much stronger than the other, for Bayezid, great-grandfather of this Selim, added a great tower to it and girt it with a double wall. In the morning the Pasha set out, resolved to come toward the Christian fleet, with two hundred and thirty royal galleys, many of them of twenty-eight and thirty banks, and seventy galliots of twenty and twenty-two banks, besides other vessels, and with so many men that, counting the ordinary complement, those who reinforced the fleet and all the rest who go on such an enterprise, they passed a hundred and twenty thousand.
units.note: The 'less than a stadium' is Herrera's; the strait at Rion is about two kilometres wide. The Ottoman celebrations of the night before are in Contarini too (Contarini Battle [1]).

sections.titel: Chapter XXV: The fleets meet at the Curzolari
sections.blurb: The signal for battle on the feast of Saint Mark, Venier's hesitation in a Spanish telling, Don John's 'not the time for counsel but for fighting', the calm and the south-east wind, and Santa Cruz's reserve.

units.orig: Están entre Lepante y la Chafalonía unos peñascos ó islas llamadas Cuzorales á ocho millas de Lepante, contrapuestas á la boca del rio Aqueloo, que hoy llaman Aspropotamo, y antiguamente fueron las islas Echinades, nacidas con el ímpetu de aquel rio de la arena y la mar, que trajo como una parte de Egito del cieno que ayuntó el Nilo. No muy lejos de aquí está aquel cabo donde Augusto César combatió en batalla naval con Marco Antonio y lo venció. A estas isletas ó peñascos enderezaba la armada de la liga con su general D. Juan de Austria, y amaneciendo muy cerca, fué navegando por ellas, y entrando por un canal, envió D. Juan á descubrir algunas fragatas en la tierra de las mesmas islas con gente prática, para que descubriesen los bajeles enemigos, y de allí hiciesen la guardia, y desembocando de las dichas islas por el canal casi á una hora de sol, en domingo dia de San Marco, pontífice y confesor, la guardia del carcés de la Real dijo que via dos velas y luego que toda la armada; y lo mismo hicieron los de tierra que estaban cerca de diez millas, y á la hora se metió la antena en cigoña con una flámula en lo alto de la pena y disparó una pieza que era la señal de la batalla.
units.en: Between Lepanto and Cephalonia there are some rocks or islands called the Curzolari, eight miles from Lepanto, facing the mouth of the river Achelous, which today they call Aspropotamo; anciently they were the Echinades islands, born of the force of that river from the sand and the sea, as a part of Egypt was brought by the mud the Nile gathered. Not far from here is the cape where Augustus Caesar fought Mark Antony in a naval battle and defeated him. Toward these islets or rocks the fleet of the League was steering with its general Don John of Austria; and, day breaking when it was very near, it sailed in among them, and, entering by a channel, Don John sent some frigates with experienced men to the land of the same islands to look out for the enemy ships and keep watch from there. And, coming out of those islands by the channel about an hour after sunrise, on Sunday, the day of Saint Mark, pope and confessor, the lookout in the masthead of the Real said he saw two sails, and then the whole fleet; and those on land, who were about ten miles off, signalled the same. At once the yard was hoisted aslant with a pennant at the peak, and a gun was fired, which was the signal for battle.
units.note: 7 October 1571 was a Sunday, the feast of Pope Saint Mark. Contarini gives the sighting 'two hours after daybreak' (Contarini Battle [2]). The Achelous has silted the Echinades almost to the shore since.

units.orig: Toda la armada con grande alegría de haber encontrado al enemigo en tan buen lugar se fué poniendo en orden, guardando el que se les habia dado, y con general contento miraban todos á la armada contraria que venia en su vuelta, bogando con mucho espacio, porque aunque al tiempo que se descubrió venia con los bastardos en popa, amainó para meterse en orden, y descubriéndose improvisamente las dos armadas á ocho ó á diez millas una de otra, pareció una maravillosa hermosura, viendo todo aquel espacio de mar cubierto de galeras que con tantos gallardetes y flámulas de varios colores resplandecían agradablemente. Aunque puso aquella vista alguna admiración en los capitanes cristianos por el orden y presteza de los turcos, ignorando que Caracosa los habia seguido y espiado de paso en paso; y así estaban algo descuidados, porque nunca tuvieron nueva cierta dellos, aunque Gil de Andrada salió dos veces á reconocellos.
units.en: The whole fleet, with great joy at having met the enemy in so good a place, put itself in order, keeping the one it had been given, and all looked with general contentment at the opposing fleet coming toward them, rowing very slowly; for although when it was sighted it was coming with its mainsails set astern, it lowered sail to get into order. And the two fleets, discovering each other suddenly at eight or ten miles, made a marvellous and beautiful sight, all that space of sea covered with galleys gleaming pleasantly with so many streamers and pennants of various colours. Although that sight caused some wonder among the Christian captains at the order and readiness of the Turks, not knowing that Kara Hoca had followed and spied on them step by step; and so they had been somewhat off their guard, for they never had certain news of them, although Gil de Andrada went out twice to reconnoitre them.

units.orig: Amaneció aquel dia con la mayor bonanza que se podia desear para tan famosa jornada, y el mar que antes se habia mostrado tan bravo que no se consentia navegar sino con grande peligro y dificultad se puso entonces tan llano y apacible que casi no parecía que se movía. Luego que oyó afirmar D. Juan que la armada del Turco se descubría, con alegre muestra de confianza imitó aquella grandeza de ánimo que Alejandro en la pasada de Asia, cuando saltó armado de la nave en la tierra de los enemigos. Y vuelto á él D. Miguel de Moncada le preguntó con mucho deseo de pelear, si pensaba combatir aquel dia. Y él respondió: ¿veis la armada enemiga tan cerca, y decís eso? Porque bien entendió que los turcos traian voluntad de la batalla por venir superiores en número de bajeles. Acudieron entonces á la galera Real todos los generales á saber la intención de su capitán, y hallándolo todos ellos tan resoluto al combate, el general Veniero que tanto lo habia deseado, conforme á lo que dicen muchos, pareció que no mostró aquella viveza y ardor que solia, dudando el suceso por la grande potencia del Turco, y también otros le representaron los peligros que nacian de su determinación, y le persuadieron que se retirase, porque se arriesgaba mucho mas á la pérdida que á la ganancia, pues se aventuraba en la dificultad de aquel suceso toda la cristiandad; y así dijeron que se consultase sobre ello.
units.en: That day dawned with the greatest calm that could be wished for so famous a day, and the sea, which before had been so rough that one could not sail without great danger and difficulty, became so flat and peaceful that it hardly seemed to move. As soon as Don John heard it affirmed that the Turk's fleet was in sight, with a cheerful show of confidence he imitated the greatness of spirit of Alexander in the crossing to Asia, when he leapt armed from the ship on to the enemy's land. And Don Miguel de Moncada, turning to him, asked him, with a great desire to fight, whether he meant to give battle that day. And he answered: 'Do you see the enemy fleet so near, and ask that?' For he understood well that the Turks came with the will to fight, being superior in number of ships. Then all the generals came to the Real to learn their captain's intention; and, finding him so resolved on battle, General Venier, who had so desired it, did not, according to what many say, seem to show the liveliness and ardour he used to, doubting the outcome because of the Turk's great power; and others too represented to him the dangers that arose from his resolution and urged him to withdraw, for he risked much more loss than gain, since all Christendom was staked on the difficulty of that outcome; and so they said it should be put to a council.
units.titel: 'Do you see the enemy fleet so near, and ask that?'
units.note: A Spanish author's doubt about the Venetian general; Contarini, a Venetian, has Venier 'armed, providing, commanding and urging' (Contarini Battle [5]) and wants a bronze statue for him (Contarini Reckoning [2]). Herrera puts the calm at dawn; Contarini at midday (Contarini Battle [9]).

units.orig: Mas él respondió generosamente que no era aquel tiempo de consejo sino de pelear, que cada uno ordenase sus galeras y escuadras, guardando la instrucción que les habia dado, y hiciesen lo que debian á caballeros y cristianos, señaladamente escogidos para servicio de Dios y reparo de la religión, porque no en vano lo habia traido la Majestad Divina en aquel estado; y saltando en una ligera fragata con Don Luis de Córdoba y Juan de Soto, fué corriendo casi por todas las galeras, metiéndolas en orden, y animando á los capitanes y soldados para combatir con aquel común enemigo de la cristiandad, poniéndoles delante la honra y valor de su nación, el premio de la vitoria y la esperanza que debian tener en Cristo, su patrón y general de aquella santa empresa. Levantóse entre toda la chusma luego un alegrísimo grito que dió á todos clara señal de la vitoria, y se encendieron los ánimos de los soldados en un ardor increible y deseo de llegar á las manos con el enemigo. Contento de aquella lozanía y brio volvió Don Juan, llevando gran número de soldados escogidos á su galera, en la cual enarbolaban los tres estandartes, y toda la armada se puso en orden con mucho concierto, porque discurrían por ella muchas fragatas con hombres de respeto que apresuraban la ordenanza, aunque se tardó en ello, habiendo remolcado las galeazas de cada cuerno y de la batalla puestas á una milla delante de la armada. Y D. Miguel de Moncada habia hecho en la Real con las velas y traspontines una pavesada y reparo contra las flechas y arcabucería del enemigo, porque en esta sazón el viento de maestro que era contrario cesó y calmó el mar como una leche, y se les pegaron á los turcos las velas en los árboles, y sobrellegó luego un poco de jaloque favorable á la armada cristiana para asaltallos con mayor vigor, y dió espacio para que se pudiesen poner en orden, y en aquella dilación gastó el Turco el tiempo en amainar y poner también en orden toda su armada, y los cristianos hicieron á gran furia las pavesadas y se armaron y pusieron en sus postas.
units.en: But he answered nobly that this was not the time for counsel but for fighting; that each should order his galleys and squadrons, keeping the instructions he had given them, and do what they owed as knights and Christians, specially chosen for the service of God and the defence of religion, for not in vain had the Divine Majesty brought him to that pass. And leaping into a light frigate with Don Luis de Córdoba and Juan de Soto, he went round almost all the galleys, putting them in order and encouraging captains and soldiers to fight that common enemy of Christendom, setting before them the honour and valour of their nation, the reward of victory and the hope they should have in Christ, their patron and general in that holy enterprise. At once a most joyful shout went up from all the rowers, which gave everyone a clear sign of victory, and the soldiers' spirits were kindled with an incredible ardour and desire to come to grips with the enemy. Pleased with that spirit and dash, Don John went back, taking a great number of picked soldiers to his galley, on which the three standards were hoisted; and the whole fleet got into order with great harmony, for many frigates with men of standing ran through it hastening the formation, although it took time, the galleasses of each wing and of the centre having been towed a mile ahead of the fleet. And Don Miguel de Moncada had made on the Real, with sails and mattresses, a pavisade and shelter against the enemy's arrows and arquebus fire; for at this time the north-west wind, which was contrary, dropped, and the sea fell calm as milk, and the Turks' sails clung to their masts; and soon after a little south-east wind came up, favourable to the Christian fleet, to attack them with greater vigour, and it gave time to get into order; and in that delay the Turk spent the time lowering sail and putting his whole fleet in order too, while the Christians made their pavisades in great haste, armed themselves and took their posts.
units.titel: 'Not the time for counsel but for fighting'
units.note: Don John's answer is in Contarini almost word for word (Contarini Battle [7]). Contarini gives the favourable wind as west-north-west; Herrera as south-east (jaloque, scirocco). The 'shout of the rowers' is the convicts'; Contarini says they were freed and armed (Contarini Battle [3]).

units.orig: El marqués de Santa Cruz, que por mandado de D. Juan habia ido con su capitana á descubrir un bajel que á las seis de la mañana pareció en las espaldas de su armada á diez millas, yendo en su caza, reconoció que era de los suyos, que no pudiendo la noche antes bogar tanto la chusma que tuviese con las escuadras, se habia quedado, y dando la vuelta á la armada que se habia alargado mas de seis millas, ya que se acercaba á ella, sintió que la Real disparó una pieza, y luego vió venir volando una fragata, enviada del general para que llegase brevemente, porque se habia descubierto la armada enemiga á ocho millas ó poco mas. Entonces el Marqués en una fragata pasó por su escuadra, ordenándola y animando á los soldados, y descargándose la galera de Francisco Morillo, veedor de las de Nápoles, de algunos impedimentos para ir mas ligera á la batalla, ya que las armadas se vian á cuatro millas, una galera veneciana que iba en la retaguardia se escurrió á la banda y echando el esquife al agua iba recogiendo todo lo que la del veedor arrojaba, deteniéndose en ello, y dejando pasar adelante el escuadrón de sus galeras. El Marqués puesto en su lugar volvióse á D. Manuel de Benavides, y D. Francisco Tello y á los demás caballeros y les dijo que aquel era dia en que los hombres de valor mostraban la nobleza de sus ánimos, y aquella ocasión era bastante para satisfacer la culpa que injustamente ponia Paulo Jovio á los cristianos en la jornada de la Prevesa, que él confiaba de todos ellos que eran tales que no tendrían necesidad de su amonestación para hacer lo que debian; y bogando sus galeras con mas furia se acercó á su batalla para poder socorrer á la parte que mas menester lo hubiese.
units.en: The Marquis of Santa Cruz, who by Don John's order had gone with his flagship to identify a vessel that appeared at six in the morning ten miles astern of his fleet, found, when he gave chase, that it was one of their own, which had fallen behind the night before because its rowers could not keep up with the squadrons. Turning back toward the fleet, which had drawn more than six miles ahead, and nearing it, he heard the Real fire a gun, and then saw a frigate come flying, sent by the general to bid him come quickly, for the enemy fleet had been sighted at eight miles or a little more. Then the Marquis went through his squadron in a frigate, ordering it and encouraging the soldiers. And when the galley of Francisco Morillo, inspector of the galleys of Naples, was lightening itself of some encumbrances to go lighter into battle, the fleets being then four miles apart, a Venetian galley of the rearguard slipped aside, put its skiff in the water and went about picking up everything the inspector's galley threw overboard, lingering over it and letting the squadron of its galleys go on ahead. The Marquis, in his place, turned to Don Manuel de Benavides, Don Francisco Tello and the other knights and told them that this was the day on which men of valour showed the nobility of their spirits, and that this occasion was enough to answer the blame that Paolo Giovio unjustly laid on the Christians for the day of Preveza; that he trusted they were all such that they would not need his admonition to do their duty. And, his galleys rowing harder, he drew near the centre, to be able to help whichever part most needed it.
units.note: The Venetian galley picking up the jettisoned stores is Herrera's jab at the Venetians. Paolo Giovio's histories had blamed the Christian commanders for Preveza (1538), the same defeat that Hasan Pasha holds up in the Ottoman council (Contarini Council [4]).

sections.titel: Chapter XXVI: The order of the fleets (abridged)
sections.blurb: Uluç Ali warns the Pasha that the western galleys will fight; the Pasha fights because Selim's order puts his head at stake. The Christian lists are left out; the Ottoman order of battle is carried.

units.orig: Ya la armada de los turcos venia tendiéndose en el mar con grande lozanía y contento de todos ellos en general, estimando en poco á sus enemigos y riéndose de la ceguedad dellos que les llevaban la presa hasta sus mesmas casas, porque al principio no podian descubrir todo el número de sus galeras, cubriendo una montaña casi la tercia parte dellas; mas después que poco á poco se descubrieron, acostándose todas, admirados de su determinación y multitud, quedaron algún tanto suspensos, y entre los hombres principales dellos y que por el uso de la guerra conocian el valor de sus contrarios, después que entendieron que las galeras del Rey Filipo, que ellos suelen llamar Ponentinas, se hallaban en aquel lugar, se temió el suceso y dicen que Ochiali dijo al Bajá que mirase bien lo que se debia hacer, porque le parecía que las galeras de poniente eran muchas y pelearian valerosamente, porque no era de creer que el Rey de España enviase á su hermano en aquella batalla sin grande consideración y esperanza de la vitoria, y con mucha gente escogida, mas que ya no era tiempo de volver atrás. Y el Bajá se resolvió de combatir por el orden expreso que tenia de Selin, que aunque fuese muy inferior y estuviese cierto de ser vencido diese la batalla, y haciendo el contrario ponia en condición de perder la cabeza, y por esta causa habia reforzado como se ha dicho su armada de tanta gente que en toda la tierra no dejó soldado, ni en Lepante quedó hombre alguno; y así no habia galera ni galeota que no trujese docientos soldados y las capitanas trecientos.
units.en: Now the Turkish fleet came on, spreading over the sea with great dash and the contentment of all of them in general, making light of their enemies and laughing at their blindness in bringing the prize to their very doors; for at first they could not discover the whole number of the Christian galleys, a mountain hiding almost a third of them. But when these came into view little by little and all drew together, the Turks, astonished at their resolution and numbers, were somewhat taken aback; and among their chief men, who knew the valour of their opponents from the practice of war, once they understood that the galleys of King Philip, which they call the Westerners, were in that place, the outcome was feared. And they say that Uluç Ali told the Pasha to consider well what should be done, for it seemed to him that the western galleys were many and would fight valiantly, since it was not to be believed that the King of Spain would send his brother into that battle without great deliberation and hope of victory, and with many picked men; but that it was now no longer time to turn back. And the Pasha resolved to fight because of the express order he had from Selim to give battle even if he were much inferior and certain to be beaten, and that if he did the contrary he put himself in danger of losing his head; and for this reason he had reinforced his fleet, as has been said, with so many men that he left no soldier in the whole country, nor any man in Lepanto; and so there was no galley or galliot that did not carry two hundred soldiers, and the flagships three hundred.
units.note: Here the Spanish account sides with the Ottoman ones against the Venetian: Uluç Ali counsels caution (Peç. Battle [6]; Tuhfe Lep. [4]), where Contarini has him press for battle (Contarini Council [8]). And the Pasha fights for fear of his head, as in Peçevî (Peç. Battle [5]). Herrera says he had the Ottoman speeches from captives.

units.orig: […] Los turcos, en cuya armada se hallaban cuarenta galeras de fanal, traian ciento y noventa y seis galeras de Constantinopla, veinte y cuatro de la Natolia, siete de Ochiali, dos de Caracosa, una de Tripol y cincuenta galeotas gruesas, de las cuales eran doce de Ochiali y una de Tripol, sin grande multitud de fustas y bergantines, y venían ordenados en media luna que parecían un extendido y grandísimo bosque; pero llegando mas cerca se repartieron en tres escuadras como los cristianos, no haciendo retaguardia. El cuerno diestro, que algunos lo hacen de cincuenta y cinco galeras y otros mucho mayor, regia Siroco, famoso cosario gobernador de Alejandría que los turcos llaman Escandería, el cual tenia con su galera en lugar opuesto al Bragadino. Seguíanse á este Selaraiz y Mahemet Bey, gobernador de Negroponto, y Caurali, y Ustref Aga y otros. El [siniestro] guiaba con los cosarios Ochiali, virey de Argel, opuesto á Juan Andrea, y Carabey su hijo y Caracial con los dos hijos de Cara Mustafá. La batalla que seria de noventa galeras tenían en medio della Alí Bajá general de mar en un hermoso bajel de veinte y nueve bancos, lleno de banderas y tres fanales, con cuatrocientos y cincuenta turcos, de los cuales eran trecientos arcabuceros y ciento flecheros. Junto á él estaba Pertau Bajá, capitán señalado en las galeras de Hungría. Extendíanse por aquella escuadra las guardas de Xío y Rodas, y los gobernadores de Tripol, de Berbería, y Galipoli, y Metelín con otros grandes personajes, tan ordenados y puestos á punto que ninguna cosa les faltaba para cierta esperanza de la vitoria.
units.en: […] The Turks, in whose fleet there were forty lantern galleys, had a hundred and ninety-six galleys of Constantinople, twenty-four of Anatolia, seven of Uluç Ali's, two of Kara Hoca's, one of Tripoli, and fifty heavy galliots, twelve of them Uluç Ali's and one of Tripoli, besides a great multitude of fustas and brigantines. They came on ordered in a half-moon, which looked like a wide and very great forest; but coming nearer they divided into three squadrons like the Christians, without a rearguard. The right wing, which some make fifty-five galleys and others much larger, was led by Scirocco, a famous corsair, governor of Alexandria, which the Turks call Iskenderiye, who had his galley opposite Barbarigo. After him came Salih Reis and Mehmed Bey, governor of Negroponte, Kara Ali, Ustref Ağa and others. The [left] was led, with the corsairs, by Uluç Ali, viceroy of Algiers, opposite Gian Andrea, with Kara Bey his son and Kara Çelebi with the two sons of Kara Mustafa. The centre, of some ninety galleys, had in its middle Ali Pasha, general at sea, in a handsome ship of twenty-nine banks, full of banners and with three lanterns, with four hundred and fifty Turks, of whom three hundred were arquebusiers and a hundred archers. Beside him was Pertev Pasha, a captain distinguished in the galleys of Hungary. Along that squadron were spread the guard galleys of Chios and Rhodes, and the governors of Tripoli, of Barbary, of Gallipoli and of Mytilene, with other great personages, so ordered and ready that they lacked nothing for a certain hope of victory.
units.note: The Christian order of battle that precedes this, galley by galley and captain by captain, is left out here […]. The print reads 'el diestro', the right, a second time; the sense requires the left, and Herrera puts Uluç Ali opposite Doria. Ali Pasha's three lanterns: Peç. Battle [7]; Kâtip Çelebi's list of the dead: Tuhfe Lep. [9].

sections.blurb: The galleasses, Ali Pasha's question whether the galleys are Venetian or from the West, his promise of freedom to his Christian rowers, the ramming of the two flagships, the Venetian wing against the shore, Barbarigo's death, Doria's manoeuvre and the Maltese flagship, and the death of Ali Pasha, mourned by his slaves.

units.orig: Estaban las armadas puestas en orden de batalla, encaradas las proas unas con otras, cuando pareciéndole á D. Juan que no marchaban parejos los dos cuernos envió al Colona para que los igualase, porque Juan Andrea se habia alargado tanto en el mar que puso en los turcos mucha esperanza, y no poca sospecha en los cristianos que no alcanzaron su intento, y así fué fama que el mismo D. Juan le envió á mandar que no se extendiese tanto, porque dejaba desabrigada la batalla. En esta sazón, que serian las once del dia, habiendo llegado el de Santa Cruz á su lugar, las galeazas comenzaron á disparar con grandísima furia y priesa, levantando las balas por cima de la agua. Los turcos, sintiendo el daño que les hacian, porque ninguna defensa podia resistir á la violencia de su ímpetu, bogaron con mucha presteza por guardarse dellas sin embestillas, porque las pensaban rendir después, y apresurando de ambas partes los remos, fueron los primeros que comenzaron la batalla los del cuerno siniestro. El Bajá, viendo aquella escuadra de galeras opuesta á su batalla, admirado de la novedad no pensada, porque nunca esperó semejante osadía en sus enemigos, preguntó si eran de Venecia, cuyas fuerzas los turcos siempre tuvieron en poco, ó si eran de poniente, y siéndole respondido que eran de poniente, se turbó, recelando el peligro que se le ofrecía con ellas.
units.en: The fleets were in battle order, prows facing prows, when Don John, thinking the two wings were not advancing level, sent Colonna to even them up; for Gian Andrea had stood so far out to sea that he gave the Turks much hope, and the Christians, who did not grasp his purpose, no little suspicion; and so the report was that Don John himself sent to order him not to spread out so far, for he was leaving the centre unprotected. At this time, which would be eleven in the morning, the Marquis of Santa Cruz having reached his place, the galleasses began to fire with the greatest fury and speed, skipping their balls over the water. The Turks, feeling the damage they did, since no defence could withstand the violence of their force, rowed very quickly to get clear of them without attacking them, for they meant to take them afterwards; and, both sides quickening their oars, the first to begin the battle were those of the left wing. The Pasha, seeing that squadron of galleys opposite his centre, astonished at the unexpected novelty, for he never expected such boldness from his enemies, asked whether they were of Venice, whose forces the Turks always held cheap, or from the West; and when he was told they were from the West, he was troubled, fearing the danger that threatened him from them.
units.titel: 'Are they Venetian, or from the West?'
units.note: Contarini's galleasses scatter a third of the fleet (Contarini Battle [10]); Herrera's Turks row past them, 'meaning to take them afterwards', and in his account the battle is won by the Spanish galleys of the centre. Kâtip Çelebi's Turks, too, fall on six ships first (Tuhfe Lep. [7]).

units.orig: Porque D. Juan de Austria habia ya mandado enderezar su galera contra la del Bajá, el cual, según afirman algunos cativos, viéndola tan grande y bien empavesada y que lo llamaba á batalla, mandó á un esclavo que reconociese que maona era aquella que venia á embestillo, y por los tres fanales y estandartes que vió le respondió que era la galera Real de España, donde venia el hermano del Rey Filipo. Entonces él, considerando su potencia y la opinión que tenia la armada otomana, juzgó que el enemigo que lo buscaba dentro en su casa venia bien armado y lleno de confianza, y con las galeras de poniente á quien tanto dudaban los turcos, temió ser perdido, y así lo dijo; tornando á preguntar si era galera de poniente, y diciéndole algunos que no embistiese á la Real cristiana, respondió: «que él no habia de hallarse sino donde hubiese mas peligro, porque en ninguna parte se podia aventurar mejor que con la Real enemiga.» Y así mandó al cómitre que cerrase con ella, y vuelto á la chusma dijo: «Si hoy es vuestro dia, Dios os lo dé, pero estad ciertos que si gano la jornada os daré libertad, por eso haced lo que debeis á las obras que habeis recibido de mí.» Desta suerte vinieron á embestirse ambas derechas, como si las trajeran con una cuerda, y fué con tanto ímpetu que la proa de la enemiga entró por cima de la de España mas de tres bancos, y se hicieron pedazos los espolones, y jamás se ha visto que los turcos embistiesen con tanto ánimo y osadía como esta vez; pero recibiólos D. Juan con tanta furia de artillería y una rociada de arcabucería que les derribó la presunción y braveza, porque á la segunda carga parecieron pocos turbantes en la popa y crujía, de los cuales venia antes muy poblada, y el capitán Domingo, que habia traido la galera Real desde Sevilla y estaba con artillería, puso tanta diligencia que disparó cinco veces en la batalla.
units.en: For Don John of Austria had already had his galley steered against the Pasha's; and the Pasha, as some captives affirm, seeing it so large and well pavised and challenging him to battle, told a slave to find out what galleass that was coming to ram him; and by the three lanterns and the standards he saw, the slave answered that it was the Royal galley of Spain, in which came King Philip's brother. Then he, considering its power and the reputation of the Ottoman fleet, judged that the enemy who sought him out in his own house came well armed and full of confidence, and, with the western galleys that the Turks so feared, he feared he was lost, and said so. Asking again whether it was a western galley, and some telling him not to attack the Christian Real, he answered 'that he must be nowhere but where the danger was greatest, for nowhere could he venture himself better than against the enemy Real.' And so he ordered the boatswain to close with it, and turning to the rowers he said: 'If today is your day, God give it you; but be sure that if I win the day I will give you your freedom; so do what you owe for the good you have received from me.' In this way the two came to ram each other head on, as if drawn by a rope, and with such force that the enemy's prow ran up over Spain's by more than three banks, and the spurs were smashed to pieces; and never have the Turks been seen to attack with such spirit and daring as this time. But Don John received them with such fury of artillery and a volley of arquebus fire that it brought down their presumption and bravado, for at the second discharge few turbans were to be seen on the poop and gangway, which before had been crowded with them; and Captain Domingo, who had brought the Real from Seville and was in charge of the artillery, was so diligent that he fired five times in the battle.
units.note: The Christian slaves at Ali Pasha's oars, promised their freedom if he won: the three lanterns that let the League find the Kapudan (Peç. Battle [7]) are here what let the Kapudan find Don John. Herrera says he had this from captives; none of it is in the Ottoman accounts.

units.orig: La del Bajá tenia por popa seis galeras que todas se acostaron á la Real cristiana, metiendo en su capitana gente de refresco. De la parte contraria tenia D. Juan á la popa, á la capitana del Comendador mayor y la Patrona de España, que sin los criados de D. Juan tenia docientos y cincuenta mosqueteros y soldados, y á la mano derecha la capitana del Papa, y á la izquierda la de Venecia; y así entre unos y otros se trabó una dudosa batalla con grandísimo ímpetu y furia, y con tan grande estruendo que no solo pareció que las galeras se hacian pedazos y quebrantaban, pero el mesmo mar, no pudiendo sustentar aquel ruido espantable, bramaba, revolviendo las ondas llenas de espuma que poco antes estaban sosegadas, y atronados los hombres no se oian, y el cielo se arrebató de los ojos de todos con la humosa oscuridad de aquellas llamas. Los turcos acometieron con grande lozanía y ferocidad puestos sus turbantes, disparando muchas balas de la escopetería y grandísimo número de flechas con tanta furia que se halló soldado atravesado peto y espaldar con una, y todos, según costumbre de gente bárbara, daban aquellos bravos alaridos y voces con que suelen espantar á sus enemigos; mas cerraron tan presto con ellos los cristianos que disparando su artillería no los dejaron aprovechar de la suya, y así se hallaron después muchos cañones de crujía cargados. La batalla se habia mezclado de tal suerte que las armadas parecían una, sin cesar un punto los arcabuces, escopetas y flechas, que ya no se oia otra cosa que el sonido dellas, ni se vía sino las astas clavadas por árboles, jarcias y antenas, porque pocas ó ninguna vez una armada contra otra se juntó en batalla con tanto furor y osadía, y nunca se acuerda la memoria de nuestros padres haber peleado con mayor contención de armas en mar, ni haber sucedido batalla en que mas gente muriese, porque en todas partes caian muertos con ostinada dureza de corazón. Como se debia esperar en la junta de tan grandes y poderosas armadas, á los unos y á los otros encendía las fuerzas la codicia de la gloria y alabanza; los unos y los otros estimaban por último grado de honra, peleando en la presencia de sus generales, mostrar cual fuese mas aventajado en fortaleza y conocimiento de la naval diciplina, y casi parecía dudoso cual era el mayor valor de los cristianos ó el de los turcos, porque estos no olvidados de su fama juzgaban por afrenta, pues les hacian ventaja en número de bajeles, no haber vencido al principio; pero los cristianos confiados en su valor proprio y en la divina piedad á quien seguían, igualando con la grandeza del ánimo á la multitud enemiga, combatían con tanta valentía que los hacían desesperar del buen suceso.
units.en: The Pasha's galley had six galleys astern of it, all of which came alongside the Christian Real, feeding fresh men into their flagship. On the other side Don John had astern the flagship of the Comendador Mayor and the Patrona of Spain, which, besides Don John's own servants, carried two hundred and fifty musketeers and soldiers, on his right hand the Pope's flagship and on his left Venice's. And so between them a doubtful battle was joined with the greatest force and fury, and with so great a din that not only did the galleys seem to be breaking and shattering, but the sea itself, unable to bear that frightful noise, roared, churning up waves full of foam that a little before had been calm; and men were deafened and could not hear one another, and the sky was snatched from everyone's eyes by the smoky darkness of those flames. The Turks attacked with great dash and ferocity, their turbans on, firing many musket balls and a great number of arrows with such fury that a soldier was found pierced through breastplate and backplate by one; and all, after the custom of barbarous people, gave those fierce yells and cries with which they are wont to frighten their enemies. But the Christians closed with them so quickly that, firing their own artillery, they did not let them use theirs, and so many bow guns were found loaded afterwards. The battle had become so mingled that the fleets seemed one, the arquebuses, muskets and arrows never ceasing for a moment, so that nothing was heard but their sound, nor anything seen but the shafts stuck in masts, rigging and yards. For seldom or never did one fleet join battle with another with such fury and daring, and the memory of our fathers does not recall a fight at sea with greater clash of arms, nor a battle in which more men died, for everywhere they fell dead with obstinate hardness of heart. As was to be expected when such great and powerful fleets met, desire for glory and praise kindled the strength of both; both held it the highest degree of honour, fighting in the presence of their generals, to show which excelled in strength and in knowledge of naval discipline; and it seemed almost doubtful which was the greater, the valour of the Christians or that of the Turks; for these, not forgetful of their fame, thought it a disgrace, since they had the advantage in number of ships, not to have won at the outset; but the Christians, trusting in their own valour and in the divine mercy they followed, matching the enemy multitude with greatness of heart, fought so bravely that they made them despair of success.
units.note: The loaded Ottoman guns found after the battle are in Contarini too (Contarini Battle [13]).

units.orig: La banda derecha de los turcos fué embestida de la izquierda de los venecianos muy cerca de tierra, y se revolvieron en una brava batalla, porque los turcos querían tomar la vuelta de la tierra para herillos por el lado, mas cerróles el paso el Barbarigo con tanta presteza, que no pudiendo conseguir su intento y haciéndoles las galeazas grande estrago y daño se pusieron en desorden con terrible confusión, porque la que iba junto á tierra llevó el timón á una galera de las que gobernaban aquel cuerno, la cual ciando se escurrió luego y tras ella las mas, y zabordaron en tierra muchas, y se comenzó á reconocer la vitoria por aquella banda primero que por otra parte, por habellos desconcertado las galeazas, aunque lo mas importante fué, porque los turcos tenían la tierra tan cerca, que los hizo, confiándose della, no pelear con la porfía que los demás, y que diese en la costa la mayor parte de sus galeras, porque ninguna cosa se pudo hacer mas acertada que, representando la batalla al enemigo dentro de su tierra, dársela junto á ella, para que se favoreciese della y no en alto mar donde la desesperación saca fuerzas.
units.en: The Turks' right wing was engaged by the Venetians' left very near the land, and they fell into a fierce battle, for the Turks wanted to go round by the land to strike them in the flank; but Barbarigo shut the passage so quickly that, unable to achieve their aim, and the galleasses doing them great slaughter and damage, they fell into disorder with terrible confusion. For the galleass nearest the land carried away the rudder of one of the galleys that led that wing, which, backing water, slipped away at once, and most of the others after it, and many ran aground; and victory began to show on that side before any other, because the galleasses had thrown them into disorder; though the most important thing was that the Turks had the land so close that, relying on it, they did not fight as stubbornly as the rest, and most of their galleys ran on to the coast. For nothing could have been done more wisely than, offering the enemy battle within his own country, to fight him close to it, so that he would rely on it, and not on the high sea, where despair draws out strength.
units.titel: The Venetian wing and the shore
units.note: The galleys run aground are in all the accounts: Contarini Battle [14]; Tuhfe Lep. [9]; the survivors who took to the mountain in Peç. Battle [8].

units.orig: La galera Santa Nicola de Nápoles, que venia en este cuerno, no disparó hasta que cerró con la enemiga que le cupo, y le llevó con la artillería toda la palamenta por un lado. Señalóse en esta galera Pedro de Malta, natural de Zaragoza, que con maravilloso ardor de ánimo incitado se arrojó dentro de la galera contraria con solo un casco y su espada con que mató cuatro bravos turcos; y Antonio de Paredes que, atravesándole una flecha toda la pierna y pasándole otra un gorjal de malla y un jaco y las lunetas de las mangas con un jubón muy estofado hasta entrar todo el hierro por el lado siniestro, saltó en la galera enemiga y peleando fué el primero que pasó adelante del árbol, pero llegando una flecha de otra galera le atravesó la garganta y cayó mal herido. El proveedor Barbarigo, que sin duda ninguna se aventajó á todos los venecianos en solicitud y trabajo con demostración de prudente y valeroso capitán, fué herido mortalmente de una flecha en un ojo, y cayendo animó generosamente á los suyos, y vivió hasta que sabiendo que la vitoria era ganada dijo: «que daba gracias á Dios que lo hubiese guardado tanto que viese vencida la batalla y roto aquel común enemigo que tanto deseó ver destruido.» Los venecianos con el dolor de su muerte y rabia de venganza peleaban animados de la ventaja que tenían los turcos, que daban al través, porque muchas veces el dolor de la afrenta y el deseo de la venganza aun á los soldados viles enciende en valor.
units.en: The galley Santa Nicola of Naples, which was in this wing, did not fire until it closed with the enemy that fell to its lot, and swept away all the oars on one side with its artillery. On this galley Pedro de Malta, a native of Saragossa, distinguished himself: fired with marvellous ardour, he threw himself into the enemy galley with only a helmet and his sword, with which he killed four brave Turks; and Antonio de Paredes, who, with one arrow through his whole leg and another through a mail gorget, a quilted jack and the elbow-plates of his sleeves and a heavily padded doublet, so that the whole iron went into his left side, leapt into the enemy galley and, fighting, was the first to get past the mast; but an arrow from another galley pierced his throat and he fell badly wounded. The provveditore Barbarigo, who without any doubt surpassed all the Venetians in care and labour, showing himself a prudent and valiant captain, was mortally wounded by an arrow in the eye; falling, he nobly encouraged his men, and lived until, learning that the victory was won, he said 'that he gave thanks to God who had kept him alive long enough to see the battle won and that common enemy broken whom he had so desired to see destroyed.' The Venetians, with grief at his death and rage for revenge, fought on, encouraged by the plight of the Turks, who were running aground; for often the pain of an affront and the desire for revenge kindle valour even in base soldiers.
units.note: Contarini: Barbarigo lost his speech at once and, hearing of the victory three days later, could only raise his hands to heaven (Contarini Battle [14]; Contarini Reckoning [2]). Herrera gives him a speech.

units.orig: Habíase alargado Ochiali tanto con el cuerno siniestro que hubo duda que no queria pelear, y pareció que era su intento cerrar los cristianos dentro de su escuadrón. Juan Andrea que se habia hecho á lo alto por ganar el viento, aunque la galeaza de aquella punta quedaba atrás, entendiendo á Ochiali hizo lo mismo, y este intento se conoció mejor después del efeto y alabó, pareciendo claro la ecelencia suya en la milicia naval, y no como publicaron algunos, á quien por su valor era odioso, y no se pudo esperar de hombre cristiano y que con tanto valor se ha mostrado en las demás empresas ofrecidas, aquel hecho verdaderamente impío, y que habia de ser aborrecido y vituperado en la memoria de todas las gentes. Por esta causa él atendía encerrar á los cosarios dentro de la batalla por no dalles lugar que embistiesen por el costado, lo cual hiciera fácilmente Ochiali, y si le huían, podía seguillos. Así se alargó tanto que dejó abierto de su escuadrón mas de dos cuerpos de galera. Conociendo Ochiali la capitana del Doria en el fanal que traia redondo, como lo estimase por gran cosario y muy diestro en milicia de mar, entendió luego que le habia alcanzado la intención, y hizo ciar bogando, y arrancó con mucha furia, sin que sus galeras disparasen pieza alguna, y atravesó por el lugar que habia dejado abierto el Doria, y se hizo al mar, y estuvo un poco mirando hasta que reconoció el estandarte de la capitana de Malta, que buscaba con quien combatir, habiendo ya rendido algunas, y con sus siete galeras dió sobre ella y se revolvió entre todas una bravísima batalla, porque los caballeros de la Religión señalados en nobleza y valor peleaban con tanta valentía que ponían en duda la esperanza de la vitoria, porque en los grandes peligros el temor acrecienta esfuerzo y osadía á los fuertes, así como dobla la cobardía á los ánimos flacos; mas al fin sobrepujados de la multitud de enemigos que sucedían continuamente, cubiertos de flechas, heridos y cansados, sin poder sustentarse mas todos los soldados con mas de cuarenta caballeros, que dellos no escaparon sino tres ó cuatro, cayeron muertos.
units.en: Uluç Ali had stood out so far with the left wing that there was doubt whether he meant to fight, and it seemed that his aim was to shut the Christians inside his squadron. Gian Andrea, who had stood out to seaward to gain the wind, although the galleass at that point was left behind, understood Uluç Ali and did the same; and this aim was better understood and praised after the event, his excellence in naval warfare being clear, and not as some published, to whom he was hateful for his valour: that deed, truly impious, which ought to be abhorred and reviled in the memory of all peoples, could not be expected of a Christian man who has shown such valour in the other enterprises that have offered. For this reason he meant to shut the corsairs inside the battle, so as not to give them room to attack him in the flank, which Uluç Ali could easily have done, and if they fled he could follow them. So he stood out so far that he left a gap in his squadron of more than two galleys' length. Uluç Ali, recognising Doria's flagship by the round lantern it carried, and holding him a great corsair and very skilled in war at sea, understood at once that he had seen through his intention, and had his men back water, and then struck out with great fury, without his galleys firing a single piece, crossed through the place Doria had left open, and put out to sea; and he stayed watching a little until he recognised the standard of the flagship of Malta, which was looking for someone to fight, having already taken some; and with his seven galleys he fell upon it, and a most fierce battle broke out among them all. For the knights of the Religion, distinguished in nobility and valour, fought so bravely that they put the hope of victory in doubt, for in great dangers fear increases the strength and daring of the brave, as it doubles the cowardice of weak spirits; but at last, overwhelmed by the multitude of enemies that kept coming on, covered with arrows, wounded and weary, unable to hold out any longer, all the soldiers, with more than forty knights, of whom no more than three or four escaped, fell dead.
units.note: Herrera defends Doria against the charge, current in Venice, that he held back on purpose; Contarini too calls his move 'a good design' (Contarini Battle [17]). The Maltese flagship and its three or four surviving knights: Cervantes's captive says 'only three knights being left alive in it' (DQ I.39 [3]); Kâtip Çelebi: Tuhfe Lep. [8].

units.orig: El prior de Mecina, que mal herido se habia retirado á curar en la cámara de popa, por persuasión de los caballeros, preso de los turcos que entraron, porque les dió los escudos que tenia, y prometió su talla, fué guardado para nueva mudanza de la fortuna, que sucedió con su libertad. En esta sazón comenzó una alegre voz en toda la armada cristiana que apellidaba vitoria. Fué la ocasión della haber acabado la Real de España de rendir á la del Turco. Habia mas de una hora que se combatía entre ellos sin conocerse vitoria, aunque los españoles ganaron dos veces hasta el árbol de la enemiga, y fueron ambas retirados por el mucho socorro que le entraba, y como D. Lope tuviese muchos heridos y muertos en la proa que estaba á su cargo, le fué á socorrer D. Bernardino de Cárdenas, y al pasar le dieron con un esmeril sobre la rodela que lo derribó atormentado y murió dello en el dia siguiente.
units.en: The Prior of Messina, who, badly wounded, had withdrawn at the knights' urging to have his wounds dressed in the stern cabin, was taken by the Turks who came aboard; because he gave them the crowns he had and promised his ransom, he was kept for a new turn of fortune, which came with his freedom. At this time a joyful voice began through the whole Christian fleet crying victory. The cause of it was that the Real of Spain had finished taking the Turk's. They had been fighting for more than an hour with no victory showing, although the Spaniards twice won as far as the enemy's mast and were twice driven back by the many reinforcements coming into her; and as Don Lope [de Figueroa] had many wounded and dead in the bow, which was in his charge, Don Bernardino de Cárdenas went to help him, and on the way a swivel-gun shot struck his buckler and threw him down stunned, and he died of it the next day.
units.titel: The cry of victory; the Real

units.orig: Peleaban en ambas Reales porfiadísimamente, acometiéndose con tanto ímpetu, que sin temor de la muerte, cada uno procuraba aventajarse, porque el que se vía atrás se juzgaba por mas flaco y de menos valor que el otro, y todos revolvían en su ánimo la grandeza de aquella vitoria, de que pendía la opinión y el imperio de la tierra y la honra de su religión; pero ya no era tan poderosa la obstinada furia y desesperada bestialidad de los turcos, cansados y fatigados con la larga batalla, y atemorizados con las muchas muertes, que pudiese hacer mas resistencia al valor y generosidad de los cristianos, porque aunque combatieron bravamente, como se esperaba de hombres que tenían tanta gloria en las armas, todos ó los mas murieron por los arcabuces y espadas de los españoles que entrando dentro consumían todo el socorro que les entraba, y mucho mas se conoció, cuando mataron á Alí Bajá, porque los esforzaba con mucho valor, yendo tres veces del estanterol al árbol, peleando con su arco. Fué su muerte llorada de los esclavos cristianos, de quien era muy amado por el buen tratamiento y humanidad que usaba con ellos. El marqués de Santa Cruz, repartiendo sus galeras para acudir donde hubiese mas necesidad, salió de su puesto á socorrer la Real, donde habia la mayor furia de la batalla, y cuando estaba en mas peligro, y allí proa con proa embistió á una galera armada de jenízaros que con otra iba á embestir á la Real por popa y entró por medio con la suya, disparando su artillería, y aferró con la que halló mas cerca, la cual hizo tanta defensa que casi toda la gente fué degollada, y el Marqués perdió algunos soldados, y á él le llegaron dos balas, una en la rodela acerada y otra en la escarcela, y no le hicieron daño ni pasaron; pero salió herido de muerte con dos arcabuzazos por las rodillas el capitán Rutia. Metiendo el Marqués gente dentro desta galera, pasó adelante y rindió otras dos, y en este tiempo la Real del Turco casi á dos horas de batalla fué presa de todo punto con muerte de mas de quinientos turcos, y derribando su estandarte fué arbolada la Cruz, á cuya vista perdieron el ánimo las galeras vecinas.
units.en: On both Reals they fought most stubbornly, attacking each other with such force that, without fear of death, each tried to outdo the other, for whoever saw himself behind thought himself weaker and of less valour than the other, and all turned over in their minds the greatness of that victory, on which hung the reputation and the empire of the earth and the honour of their religion. But the obstinate fury and desperate savagery of the Turks, tired and worn out by the long battle and terrified by the many deaths, was no longer strong enough to resist the valour and nobility of the Christians any longer; for although they fought bravely, as was to be expected of men who had such glory in arms, all or most of them died by the arquebuses and swords of the Spaniards, who, getting aboard, used up all the reinforcements that came to them; and this was all the more evident when they killed Ali Pasha, for he urged them on with great valour, going three times from the stern-post to the mast, fighting with his bow. His death was mourned by the Christian slaves, by whom he was much loved for the good treatment and humanity he showed them. The Marquis of Santa Cruz, dividing his galleys to go where there was most need, left his post to help the Real, where the fury of the battle was greatest, at the moment of greatest danger; and there, prow to prow, he rammed a galley full of Janissaries that was about to attack the Real from astern with another, went in between them with his own, firing his artillery, and grappled the nearer one, which defended itself so hard that almost all its men were cut down; and the Marquis lost some soldiers, and two balls struck him, one on his steel buckler and another on his tasset, and did him no harm and did not pass through; but Captain Rutia came out mortally wounded with two arquebus shots through the knees. Putting men into this galley, the Marquis went on and took two more; and at this time the Turk's Real, after almost two hours of battle, was taken entirely, with the death of more than five hundred Turks; and, its standard being struck, the Cross was raised, at the sight of which the neighbouring galleys lost heart.
units.note: Ali Pasha 'mourned by the Christian slaves': a Spanish historian's tribute to the enemy commander. Peçevî gives the Kapudan's valour ('he fought with great valour and in the first onset fell upon the infidel fleet', Peç. Battle [7]); Kâtip Çelebi calls him brave but ignorant of the sea (Tuhfe Lep. [5]). The Cross raised on the Ottoman flagship is the image of the prints and medals that followed.

units.orig: Y entonces los turcos heridos de inmenso temor guardaban menos el orden militar, porque, declinando la fortuna, también declinaba aquella braveza y ferocidad con que combatían, aunque en algunas partes fué tanta la pertinacia de sus ánimos que primero quisieron morir ó ser presos por otra fuerza que tentar la huida, y así, no rindiéndose, pasaban todos á cuchillo. Venia en esta sazón la galera de los hijos del Bajá Mahemet Bey y Saín Bey buscando á su padre, cuando la capitana del Comendador mayor se afrontó con ella, y entre ambas se revolvió una sangrienta escaramuza, de la cual quedó herido con una flecha en los pechos D. Juan Mejía, hermano del marqués de la Guardia. Al fin, aunque los turcos peleaban con grande fortaleza y defendían con valor maravilloso la entrada, fué tanto el ímpetu de los españoles animados de D. Alejandro Torrellas y D. Fernando de Sayavedra que á fuerza de brazos entraron dentro con cruel estrago de los infieles que sin poder hacer resistencia caían traspasados de las balas y hechos pedazos de las espadas enemigas. Y fueron presos de los caballeros, no queriendo rendirse á otros, los hijos del Bajá que por su tierna edad reservados del peligro de las armas estaban en las cámaras de popa con su ayo esperando la muerte.
units.en: And then the Turks, struck with immense fear, kept military order less, for, as fortune declined, so did that bravery and ferocity with which they fought; though in some places their stubbornness was so great that they preferred to die or be taken by force rather than attempt flight, and so, not surrendering, all were put to the sword. At this time the galley of the Pasha's sons, Mehmed Bey and Said Bey, came looking for their father, when the flagship of the Comendador Mayor came face to face with it, and a bloody skirmish broke out between them, in which Don Juan Mejía, brother of the Marquis of La Guardia, was wounded by an arrow in the chest. At last, although the Turks fought with great strength and defended the entry with marvellous valour, such was the force of the Spaniards, led on by Don Alejandro Torrellas and Don Fernando de Saavedra, that by strength of arm they got aboard with cruel slaughter of the infidels, who, unable to resist, fell pierced by bullets and cut to pieces by the enemy swords. And the Pasha's sons, who because of their tender age had been kept from the danger of arms and were in the stern cabins with their tutor awaiting death, were taken by the knights, not wishing to surrender to others.
units.note: Peçevî: 'his sons were taken with the bastarda' (Peç. Battle [7]); Kâtip Çelebi: 'his two sons and those aboard were taken prisoner' (Tuhfe Lep. [7]).

sections.blurb: The rest of the line, Uluç Ali's flight with the standard of Malta, the rout on the shore and a Turk impaled by a Venetian, the sea on fire in the rain, the count, and the judgement: greater than Salamis and Actium, if the League holds and does not let Selim rebuild.

units.orig: Marco Antonio Colona, acompañado de los caballeros napolitanos y coloneses, combatió bravamente con dos galeras rindiendo algunos bajeles con pérdida de algunos caballeros, y en aquella ocasión mostraron todos que aun no era muerto aquel antiguo valor de los ánimos italianos, porque muchos con deseo de vengar las injurias comunes en aquellos fieros enemigos de la religión cristiana ecedieron todas las esperanzas que se tenían de su fortaleza, y la galera Elbicina que venia al gobierno de Honorato ganó á la hermosa galera de la Guardia de Rodas que traia docientos y cincuenta soldados, y el capitán Juan Batista Cortés que estaba en ella mató por su mano á Caracosa que regia una grande y bien arreada galera con un hermosísimo fanal y ciento y cincuenta turcos de guerra, aunque otros atribuyen á la galera Grifona del Papa el vencimiento de Caracosa, que se afrontó con él, que junto á sí tenía á Alí, capitán, con su galeota, y comenzaron el asalto con tanta braveza que, no pudiendo los turcos meter pie en la Grifona fueron entrados y hechos pedazos con Caracosa, y la Toscana rindió á la del pagador del Turco, la cual era la capitana de Pío Cuarto, que fué presa en los Gelves con Flaminio de la Anguilara, caballero romano, que con tres de la iglesia fué en aquella jornada. La capitana de Lomelin donde iba Paulo Jordán Ursino peleó en diversas veces con algunas galeras, y el Ursino, señalándose con mucho valor, fué herido poco en una pierna de una flecha cansada y Troilo Sabelo; pero salió mal herido el caballero Arrigi, y el Espinosa, y Julio Naldino y Horacio Ursino con dos arcabuzazos en un muslo, con otros treinta soldados, y murieron el caballero Berardo, y peleando valerosamente Virgilio Ursino de un escopetazo que le pasó la rodela y el coselete con otros cinco ó seis soldados.
units.en: Marcantonio Colonna, with the Neapolitan knights and his own Colonna men, fought bravely with two galleys, taking some ships with the loss of some knights; and on that occasion all showed that the ancient valour of Italian spirits was not yet dead, for many, desiring to avenge the common injuries on those fierce enemies of the Christian religion, exceeded every hope that had been held of their courage. The galley Elbigina, commanded by Onorato, took the handsome guard galley of Rhodes, which carried two hundred and fifty soldiers; and Captain Giovanni Battista Cortese, who was on it, killed with his own hand Kara Hoca, who commanded a large and well-fitted galley with a most handsome lantern and a hundred and fifty Turkish fighting men; although others credit the Pope's galley Grifona with the defeat of Kara Hoca, who engaged it, having beside him Ali, a captain, with his galliot; and they began the assault so fiercely that, the Turks being unable to set foot on the Grifona, they were boarded and cut to pieces with Kara Hoca. And the Toscana took the galley of the Turk's paymaster, which had been Pius IV's flagship, taken at Djerba with Flaminio dell'Anguillara, a Roman knight, who went on that expedition with three galleys of the Church. The flagship of Lomellini, with Paolo Giordano Orsini aboard, fought several times with various galleys; and Orsini, distinguishing himself with great valour, was slightly wounded in the leg by a spent arrow, and Troilo Savelli too; but the knight Arrighi came out badly wounded, and Spinosa, and Giulio Naldini, and Orazio Orsini with two arquebus shots in the thigh, with thirty other soldiers; and there died the knight Berardo, and, fighting valiantly, Virgilio Orsini, from a musket shot that went through his buckler and his corselet, with five or six other soldiers.
units.note: Kara Hoca, the spy who counted the League short (Herrera Search [3]; Contarini Council [2]), dies in the battle; Kâtip Çelebi's list of the dead does not name him (Tuhfe Lep. [9]). The paymaster's galley that had been Pius IV's: taken at Djerba in 1560, retaken now.

units.orig: Juan Andrea Doria, en cuyo cuerno las galeras padecían mucho por tener contra sí á los cosarios, porque por aquella banda tendidos en largo mar, y sin que las galeazas, que llegaron tarde, hiciesen mucha ofensa, pelearon hasta las cuatro, que allí se hallaron galeras enemigas, que combatieron bravísimamente y con furia desatinada que apena se les podía resistir, viendo que Ochiali se le habia apartado y que le estaba alargando en alto, por cerrar al Turco, miró donde habia mas necesidad de socorro, y dió la vuelta y embistió las galeras que halló por delante y rindió por fuerza dos dellas, y viniendo otra á abordar con él la Imperial de Sicilia que le iba de socorro, donde venia la compañía de Juan de Angulo, le asestó un cañón que la metió á fondo. Estando el Doria en el estanterol, animando á los soldados, una pieza le mató al espalder y lo tiñó con la sangre dél, y pasando la bala debajo sus pies rompió el estanterol. Corrió semejante peligro Otavio Gonzaga, porque estando fuera de la galera en la fragata con alguna gente para pelear sin impedimento de los otros, faltó poco para que lo matase una pieza que le pasó apartada casi un palmo y le despedazó delante dos criados, rompiendo de una á otra banda el reparo de la fragata y parte de la galera; mas aunque Juan Andrea lo procurase mucho rehuyó siempre Ochiali encontrarse con él, de suerte que ambos se hallaron siempre en parte diferente. Don Juan de Cardona, que con las ocho galeras tenía cargo de hacer guardia y descubrir el mar, y entonces se habia adelantado con cuatro, llegó mezclada ya la batalla, y acercándose á su lugar lo halló abierto por donde querían pasar mas de quince galeras contrarias, y por excusar el daño que podía resultar se afrontó con ellas, peleando muy grande espacio sin que le entrase alguna. Su capitana padeció mucho peligro y quedó cuajada de flechas por todo el tendal y fanal, por el árbol y antenas, y las arrumbadas mas que ninguna de todas las galeras. Murió en ella el Comendador Heredia del hábito de San Juan y D. Jorge de Rebolledo. Su capitán fué mortalmente herido y quemadas las caras y manos de fuegos artificiales D. Juan Osorio y D. Fernando de la Águila y mas de ciento y cincuenta soldados entre muertos y heridos; pero defendió su galera el mesmo D. Juan con mucho valor, herido de una flecha y atormentado de la furia de una escopeta, que le dió en los pechos sobre un peto fuerte que el Príncipe de Toscana le habia dado en Génova. Fué allí la batalla tan peligrosa que de quinientos españoles que metió en aquellas galeras D. Diego Enriquez de su tercio, no quedaron cincuenta sanos, ni oficial alguno.
units.en: Gian Andrea Doria's wing suffered much, having the corsairs against it; for on that side, spread out over the open sea, and without the galleasses, which arrived late, doing much damage, they fought until four o'clock, enemy galleys being there that fought most bravely and with such wild fury that they could hardly be resisted. Seeing that Uluç Ali had drawn away from him and was standing out to sea to shut in the Turk [sic], Doria looked where help was most needed, turned, attacked the galleys he found before him and took two of them by force; and when another came to board him, the Imperial of Sicily, which was coming to his help with Juan de Angulo's company aboard, trained a cannon on it and sank it. While Doria was at the stern-post encouraging the soldiers, a shot killed his stroke-oar man beside him and stained him with his blood, and the ball, passing under his feet, broke the stern-post. Ottavio Gonzaga ran a like danger, for, being out of the galley in the frigate with some men to fight without hindering the others, he was very nearly killed by a shot that passed a hand's breadth from him and tore apart two of his servants before him, breaking the frigate's bulwark from side to side and part of the galley's. But, much as Gian Andrea tried, Uluç Ali always avoided meeting him, so that the two were always in different places. Don Juan de Cardona, who with the eight galleys was charged with keeping watch and scouting the sea, and had gone ahead with four, arrived when the battle was already joined, and, drawing near his place, found it open, where more than fifteen enemy galleys wanted to pass; and to prevent the damage that could follow he engaged them, fighting for a very long time without any of them boarding him. His flagship was in great danger and was left bristling with arrows all over the awning and lantern, the mast and yards, and the bow platforms more than any other galley. Knight Commander Heredia of the habit of Saint John and Don Jorge de Rebolledo died on her. Her captain was mortally wounded; Don Juan Osorio and Don Fernando de la Águila had their faces and hands burned by fireworks, and more than a hundred and fifty soldiers were killed or wounded; but Don Juan himself defended his galley with great valour, wounded by an arrow and shaken by the force of a musket shot that struck him in the chest on a strong breastplate the Prince of Tuscany had given him in Genoa. The battle there was so dangerous that of five hundred Spaniards of his tercio whom Don Diego Enríquez put into those galleys, not fifty remained unhurt, nor any officer.
