units.note: 'To shut in the Turk': Herrera means Uluç Ali; the printed text says 'el Turco'. Contarini praises Cardona for saving himself 'fighting' among the galleys mauled by Uluç Ali (Contarini Reckoning [2]).

units.orig: Mas la Florencia del Papa, adelantándose demasiadamente y asaltada de cuatro galeras sin ser socorrida, quedó inútil para ejercitar mas la navegación, porque muriendo en ella con miserable estrago todos los soldados, y marineros, y forzados y los caballeros del orden de San Esteban, como el León y el Quistelo, el Bonaguisi y Tornabuoni, el Salutato y el capitán Juan María Pucini y otros que allí habia, eceto Tomás de Médicis, capitán de la dicha galera, atravesado el brazo de una bala y quemados del fuego del martel, y el Reniero con no poco peligro de la vida y otros quince hombres que escaparon heridos y maltratados. Casi el mesmo daño padeció en los soldados y hombres de cabo la galera San Juan del Papa, sacando dos arcabuzazos en la gola el capitán Angelo Bisolo, que la gobernaba. Después de rendida la Real del Turco D. Juan de Austria fué de parecer con el Comendador mayor que socorriesen á las del cuerno diestro, que aun peleaban; pero jamás quiso ayudar alguna que no tuviese encontrados enemigos, porque no se dijese que su Real algunas veces se halló con ventaja, y rindiendo á una seguía luego las que huían, y así yendo en seguimiento de muchas las compelía que fuesen á dar al través, y desta suerte se mudó la fortuna de todo punto con su llegada, y los turcos que combatían con tanto valor súbitamente perdieron todo el ánimo que tenían y desmayando todos no podían sufrir el ímpetu de los cristianos, y el estruendo de la artillería, y arcabucería y el ruido de las armas, y las voces de los que peleaban los turbaban y angustiaban, entorpeciéndolos Ochiali que, según muchos afirman, nunca peleó con su galera. Viendo que llegaba socorro á la de Malta se retiró á la batalla y hallando todas las cosas en desorden, huyó con el estandarte de la Religión. Socorrida la capitana de Malta fué conocida por la imagen de la sagrada Madre de Dios que traia arrimada al fanal. Su Patrona la remolcó y enarboló otro estandarte, hallándose muertos en ella mas de trecientos turcos; y el prior de Mecina cobrando la libertad perdida ganó los escudos que dió á los turcos y á ellos por sus esclavos, que por no caer en mas crueles manos se le dieron.
units.en: But the Pope's Florence, pushing too far ahead and attacked by four galleys without being helped, was left unfit to sail any further: all the soldiers, sailors and convicts died on her in miserable slaughter, with the knights of the order of Saint Stephen, such as Leone and Quistello, Bonaguisi and Tornabuoni, Salutati and Captain Giovanni Maria Puccini and others who were there, except Tommaso de' Medici, captain of the said galley, his arm pierced by a bullet and burned by the fire of the martel [?], and Renieri, with no small danger to his life, and fifteen other men who escaped wounded and battered. The Pope's galley San Giovanni suffered almost the same loss among its soldiers and officers, its captain Angelo Bisolo taking two arquebus shots in the gorget. After the Turk's Real had been taken, Don John agreed with the Comendador Mayor to help those of the right wing, which were still fighting; but he would never help any galley that had not got enemies engaged, so that it should not be said that his Real had ever fought at an advantage; and, taking one, he at once followed those that fled, and so, pursuing many, forced them to run aground. And in this way fortune turned completely with his arrival; and the Turks, who had fought with such valour, suddenly lost all the spirit they had, and, all fainting, could not bear the onset of the Christians; the thunder of the artillery and arquebuses, the noise of arms and the shouts of the fighters troubled and distressed them; and Uluç Ali, who, as many affirm, never fought with his own galley, hampered them. Seeing that help was coming to the Maltese galley, he withdrew toward the centre, and, finding everything in disorder, fled with the standard of the Religion. The flagship of Malta, once relieved, was recognised by the image of the holy Mother of God that it carried beside its lantern. Its Patrona took it in tow and hoisted another standard, more than three hundred Turks being found dead on it; and the Prior of Messina, recovering his lost freedom, won back the crowns he had given the Turks, and the Turks themselves as his slaves, who gave themselves up to him so as not to fall into crueller hands.
units.titel: Uluç Ali flees with the standard of Malta
units.note: The 'martel' is printed so and not understood here. 'Uluç Ali never fought with his own galley': a Spanish charge against the Ottoman hero, whom the Ottoman historians praise for fighting his way out (Tuhfe Lep. [8]; Peç. Battle [9]). The standard of Malta went to Istanbul (DQ I.39 [4]).

units.orig: Reconocida ya la vitoria en todas partes á las cuatro del dia, aunque el humo de la artillería no daba lugar, el marqués de Santa Cruz descubrió cuarenta galeras que con el trinquete se salían de la batalla y tomaban la vuelta de Lepanto. Entonces él con otras dos galeras suyas atravesó por medio de la armada, dándoles caza el primero de todos, rindiendo algunas y dejando soldados dentro. Seguíale Juan Andrea con su Patrona y la de David Imperial y D. Alonso Bazan con su capitana, y todos estos yendo en alcance con la Real, que iba junta con la del Marqués, las hicieron embestir en tierra, porque solas cinco ó seis se alargaron, no osando las demás que temieron que las seguiría toda la armada, y estaban todos tan medrosos y quebrantados viéndose rotos, que pudiendo salvarse en el puerto de Lepanto que tenían tan cerca, dieron vergonzosamente en tierra y con la agua á la garganta se metieron en su costa. Sucedió entonces que dando caza la capitana de Nápoles á una que zabordó en tierra, llegó otra veneciana en alcance de una, y embistiendo juntamente en tierra con la de Nápoles, y arrojándose al agua todos los turcos, algunos venecianos con deseo de matallos, hicieron lo mesmo, y adelantándose uno con solo un palo en la mano alcanzó á uno de aquellos turcos que huían, y de dos ó tres golpes dió con él en tierra junto al agua entre unas peñas, y abriéndole la boca lo enclavó en el palo con tanta fiereza y rabia de ánimo endurecido, que aun en los suyos puso lástima aquel nuevo y crudo género de muerte. Duró el rendimiento y saco de las galeras hasta la noche que se arrimó á la tierra, quemando muchos bajeles enemigos con un espectáculo alegrísimo, porque la noche sucedió oscurísima y con grande pluvia; parecía el mar ardiendo en llamas un monte de fuego, y en todo el espacio de la batalla se vió teñido en sangre infiel y cristiana, lleno de cuerpos muertos y despedazados de varias maneras, y cubierto de bajeles rotos, de fuegos, de remos, de astas y armas, que ningún suceso se pudo ver de mayor terribilidad, ni mas digna consideración de la miseria humana.
units.en: The victory being now recognised on every side at four in the afternoon, although the smoke of the artillery hardly allowed it, the Marquis of Santa Cruz discovered forty galleys leaving the battle under their foresails and making for Lepanto. Then he, with two more of his galleys, cut through the middle of the fleet, the first of all to give chase, taking some and leaving soldiers aboard. Gian Andrea followed him with his Patrona and that of David Imperiale, and Don Alonso Bazán with his flagship; and all these, pursuing with the Real, which was with the Marquis's, made them run ashore; for only five or six stood out to sea, the rest not daring, fearing that the whole fleet would follow them; and they were all so fearful and broken, seeing themselves beaten, that, though they could have saved themselves in the harbour of Lepanto so near at hand, they shamefully ran aground and, with the water up to their throats, made for their own coast. It happened then that, the flagship of Naples chasing one that ran aground, a Venetian galley came up in pursuit of another and ran aground together with the one from Naples; and, all the Turks throwing themselves into the water, some Venetians did the same in their desire to kill them; and one of them, going ahead with nothing but a stake in his hand, caught one of the fleeing Turks, knocked him down with two or three blows on the shore by the water among some rocks, and, forcing his mouth open, drove the stake through him with such ferocity and rage of a hardened heart that that new and cruel kind of death moved even his own companions to pity. The surrender and sack of the galleys lasted until nightfall, when they drew in to land, burning many enemy ships in a most joyful spectacle; for the night came on very dark and with heavy rain. The sea, burning in flames, looked like a mountain of fire, and the whole space of the battle was seen stained with infidel and Christian blood, full of dead bodies torn apart in many ways, and covered with broken ships, fires, oars, shafts and arms, so that no event could be seen of greater terror, nor more worthy of reflection on human misery.
units.titel: The flight; a Turk impaled; the sea on fire
units.note: The forty galleys that fled are Uluç Ali's and those that escaped with him (Contarini Reckoning [4]). The impaling is told by a Spanish author of a Venetian soldier; Contarini, a Venetian, says only that the Christians of the left wing 'left no infidel alive' (Contarini Battle [14]). Contarini's storm comes after nightfall (Contarini Battle [19]).

units.orig: Murieron de los turcos, según en estas cosas es la fama incierta y amiga de acrecentar los hechos, casi veinte mil, y fueron presos pocos mas de dos mil, y entre estos Siroco, famoso cosario y virey de Alejandría; fué esclavo de Juan Contarino. Todos los demás capitanes señalados y oficiales, de quien se hacia estimación entre ellos, murieron peleando, que solo Ochiali escapó y Pertau, el cual no se supo si era muerto ó herido, antes se creía que hubiese ido á fondo con su galera. Cobraron libertad mas de doce mil esclavos cristianos y entre ellos se halló parte de los presos en Dulcino y Antibari. Perdieron los turcos casi docientos y cuarenta bajeles, que pocos mas de cincuenta pudieron huir, porque se hallaron por popa de la armada cristiana mas de ciento y sesenta galeras sin las que se quemaron y dieron al través, y sin las demás galeotas ganadas; y de las de fanal se cree que no escaparon tres; y nunca aquella ferocísima gente recibió tan grande herida, con la cual pagó en un dia todos los daños hechos, y pareció cosa maravillosa que así como á Solimano solo el Emperador Cárlo Quinto pudo hacer huir afrentosamente, así al hijo Selin su hijo D. Juan pudiese vencer solo; pero apena se pudo creer tanta multitud de bajeles ser rotos y presos con no igual daño de los vencedores, los cuales creían que no por fuerza humana, sino por divina Providencia habían ganado aquella vitoria, porque tan grande armada, peleando con tanto valor, no se entendía que podía ser deshecha por fortaleza de hombres, y parecía que ya había venido tiempo en que no solo se había de conquistar la nobilísima ciudad de Constantinopla, pero el antiguo nombre de los Príncipes otomanos había de ser destruido, porque en aquella infelice batalla perdía Selin la reputación ganada en tantas empresas, por ser su armada mayor y haberse prometido la vitoria, estando puesto en el mas supremo grado de su gloria.
units.en: Of the Turks there died, as far as report, uncertain in such things and fond of enlarging deeds, can tell, nearly twenty thousand, and little more than two thousand were taken, among them Scirocco, the famous corsair and viceroy of Alexandria; he became the slave of Giovanni Contarini. All the other distinguished captains and officers of any account among them died fighting; only Uluç Ali escaped, and Pertev, of whom it was not known whether he was dead or wounded; rather it was believed he had gone down with his galley. More than twelve thousand Christian slaves recovered their freedom, and among them were found some of those taken at Dulcigno and Antivari. The Turks lost nearly two hundred and forty ships, for little more than fifty could escape: more than a hundred and sixty galleys were found in tow of the Christian fleet, besides those burned and run aground, and besides the galliots taken; and of the lantern galleys it is believed that not three escaped. Never did that most ferocious people receive so great a wound, with which it paid in one day for all the harm it had done; and it seemed a marvellous thing that, as the Emperor Charles V alone could make Suleiman flee in disgrace, so his son Don John alone could defeat Suleiman's son Selim. But it could hardly be believed that such a multitude of ships had been broken and taken without equal loss to the victors, who believed they had won that victory not by human strength but by divine Providence; for so great a fleet, fighting with such valour, could not be understood to be destroyed by the strength of men; and it seemed that the time had come when not only the most noble city of Constantinople was to be conquered, but the ancient name of the Ottoman princes was to be destroyed; for in that unhappy battle Selim lost the reputation won in so many enterprises, his fleet being the greater and he having promised himself the victory, set at the very summit of his glory.
units.note: Herrera's count: twelve thousand Christians freed, the figure the game rounds up to fifteen thousand. Scirocco, whom Herrera has taken alive, died of his wounds by other accounts. Pertev 'believed to have gone down with his galley': he escaped ashore (Contarini Battle [16]; Peç. Battle [7]). Compare the counts: #/compare/count.

units.orig: Pero no fué el vencimiento sin sangre, aunque templaba el daño común la alegría de tan insignes despojos y la grandeza que prometían de su vitoria, porque ninguna gloria les podía suceder mayor que haber postrado la ferocidad de aquel superbísimo enemigo, y que siempre se podían quejar de la fama como falta ó maliciosa que dilatando siempre y acrecentando en mas todas las cosas, para explicar esta vitoria habría de parecer torpe y ruda. Muchas galeras cristianas salieron tan maltratadas que era necesario remolcallas, otras bogaban diez ó doce remos, y cual veinte ó treinta, y fueron perdidas dos del Pontífice y otras tantas de Sicilia y del Doria, y la Piamontesa de Saboya degollada en ella toda la gente de cabo y remo y despedazado con once heridas D. Francisco de Saboya, y mas de otras diez de Venecia; pero no se perdió alguna que no se recobrase. Y fué afirmación de muchos que en ninguna de las catorce de España metió el pié jamás turco alguno, porque todas iban llenas de gente escogida y en cada una mas de docientos soldados. Los que murieron en aquel furor de armas llegaron al número de cuatro mil, y con los heridos casi siete mil, sin los que cobraron salud de sus heridas que fueron muchos. Entre los que perdieron la vida se contaron algunos estimados capitanes españoles […] y de los venecianos faltaron muchos nobles como el Lorenzo y Antonio Pascualigo, Vincencio Quirino y Marco Antonio Lando, el Malipiero, y Gerónimo Contarino y otros con D. Gaspar de Toraldo, coronel por la Señoría de mil y docientos infantes. […] Pero al marqués de Santa Cruz por parecer y confesión de todos se le debe atribuir mucha parte de la vitoria, porque socorrió á la Real y en muchas partes con grandísimo valor, cumpliendo con el cargo que tenía y con la confianza que D. Juan de Austria hacia dél.
units.en: But the victory was not without blood, though the common loss was tempered by the joy of such notable spoils and the greatness they promised from the victory; for no greater glory could befall them than to have laid low the ferocity of that most proud enemy; and they could always complain of report as deficient or malicious, for, while always stretching and enlarging all things, it would seem clumsy and crude in telling this victory. Many Christian galleys came out so battered that they had to be towed; others rowed with ten or twelve oars, some with twenty or thirty; two of the Pope's were lost, as many of Sicily and of Doria's, and the Piemontese of Savoy, with all her officers and rowers cut down and Don Francesco of Savoy hacked to pieces with eleven wounds, and more than ten others of Venice; but none was lost that was not recovered. And many affirmed that no Turk ever set foot in any of the fourteen galleys of Spain, for all were full of picked men, more than two hundred soldiers in each. Those who died in that fury of arms reached the number of four thousand, and with the wounded nearly seven thousand, not counting those who recovered from their wounds, who were many. Among those who lost their lives were some esteemed Spanish captains […]; and of the Venetians many nobles were missing, such as Lorenzo and Antonio Pasqualigo, Vincenzo Quirini and Marc'Antonio Lando, Malipiero and Girolamo Contarini and others, with Don Gaspar de Toraldo, colonel of twelve hundred infantry for the Signoria. […] But to the Marquis of Santa Cruz, by the opinion and admission of all, a great part of the victory must be attributed, for he helped the Real and many other places with the greatest valour, fulfilling the charge he had and the confidence Don John placed in him.
units.note: The list of the Spanish dead and the praise of individual commanders are shortened here […]. 'No Turk ever set foot in any of the fourteen galleys of Spain': a national claim. Contarini's Christian dead: 7,656 (Contarini Reckoning [3]); Herrera's: four thousand.

units.orig: Desta suerte tuvo fin la mayor batalla que ha habido en mar, porque ninguna de los antiguos se le puede comparar, pues las de los griegos no merecen ser conferidas con ella, y si la mayor que tuvieron y mas celebraron con inmortales escritos de maravillosa elocuencia fué la de Salamina, dejando aparte la multitud de bajeles que en ninguna cosa se igualan con los desta edad, en todo es diferente della en grandeza y en aparato de armas y orden de guerra. Los romanos que pusieron la milicia en mas perfecion, y con perpetuo curso de vitorias domaron las soberbias cervices y ánimos de gentes bravas y belicosas, y no contentos con la gloria ganada en la tierra, acometieron por mar empresas dignas de eterno nombre, aunque levantaron con la grandeza y felicidad de sus ingenios las jornadas navales, poniendo por testimonio la ilustre vitoria que Augusto César alcanzó de Marco Antonio, en la cual estaba pendiente el imperio de las tierras, solo en el peso de lo que se aventuraba se puede conferir con esta batalla, que también fué de un imperio á otro, cosa pocas veces vista, y entre turcos, gente de tanto valor, y españoles é italianos que nunca perdieron la fortaleza envejecida en sus ánimos; pero en lo demás le es grandemente inferior, porque, no negando la milicia y diciplina romana y el valor antiguo, todos los bajeles están ahora en mayor orden y concierto, y la navegación es mas fácil y tratable, por el mucho uso que hay, y los que siguen la milicia naval tienen mas conocimiento della y se hallan en mas fortunas y trances. Pues las batallas de mar ¿quién duda que no sean ahora mas peligrosas? […] Pero ahora un cañón de crujía abre de proa á popa un bajel. Esto es, si yo no me engaño, lo que confirma mi opinión. Otros juzgarán otra cosa, pero no negarán, si la pasión de ánimos enemigos de nuestro tiempo no lo impide, que la grandeza desta vitoria no sea mayor y mas justamente merecedora de la inmortalidad de la memoria que todas las que han sido en todos los senos del Mediterráneo, y que la felicidad della promete nuevo imperio á la religión cristiana, si los que tan santamente juntaron sus fuerzas contra la impiedad y furor de los turcos, perseveran como celosos de la honra divina y no conceden lugar á Selin para que se rehaga del daño recibido, porque su poder es tan grande que fácilmente puede cubrir las ondas con infinita multitud de bajeles; mas si dichosamente siguen los principios de su fortuna, será compelido á desamparar la Grecia, y temiendo el peligro que le amenaza, huir en la Natolia para seguridad de su vida.
units.en: So ended the greatest battle there has been at sea, for none of the ancients can be compared with it. The battles of the Greeks do not deserve to be set beside it; and if the greatest they had, and celebrated most with immortal writings of marvellous eloquence, was Salamis, leaving aside the multitude of ships, which are in no way equal to those of this age, it is in everything different from this one in greatness, in apparatus of arms and in order of war. The Romans, who brought the art of war to its greatest perfection, and in a perpetual course of victories tamed the proud necks and spirits of brave and warlike peoples, and, not content with the glory won on land, undertook at sea enterprises worthy of eternal fame; although they raised naval battles high with the greatness and felicity of their genius, setting up as witness the famous victory Augustus Caesar won over Mark Antony, on which hung the empire of the world; only in the weight of what was ventured can that be compared with this battle, which was also between one empire and another, a thing seldom seen, and between Turks, a people of such valour, and Spaniards and Italians, who never lost the strength grown old in their spirits; but in everything else it is greatly inferior. For, without denying the Roman art of war and discipline and the valour of old, all ships are now in greater order and harmony, navigation is easier and more manageable through much use, and those who follow the naval profession have more knowledge of it and meet more storms and dangers. As for battles at sea, who doubts that they are now more dangerous? […] But now a bow gun opens a ship from stem to stern. This, unless I am mistaken, is what confirms my opinion. Others will judge otherwise; but they will not deny, unless the passion of hostile spirits in our time prevents it, that the greatness of this victory is greater and more justly deserving of immortal memory than all that have been in all the bays of the Mediterranean; and that its happiness promises a new empire to the Christian religion, if those who so holily joined their forces against the impiety and fury of the Turks persevere, zealous for the divine honour, and give Selim no room to recover from the damage received; for his power is so great that he can easily cover the waves with an infinite multitude of ships. But if they happily follow up the beginnings of their fortune, he will be compelled to abandon Greece and, fearing the danger that threatens him, flee into Anatolia for the safety of his life.
units.titel: Greater than Salamis and Actium, if the League holds
units.note: A passage comparing ancient and modern arms is shortened […]. Herrera's condition, written in September 1572, is the game's question. Selim did cover the waves with ships within the winter (Peç. Fleet [4]; Tuhfe Fleet [2]); the League did not persevere; Venice made its peace six months after this was printed (Liga Faith [6]). The superlatives on each side: #/compare/count.

sections.titel: Canción: Let us sing to the Lord
sections.blurb: Herrera's song of victory, printed with the Relación: twenty stanzas and an envoi after the Song of Moses and the Psalms, the Sultan as Pharaoh and Tyre, Don John as the Lion out of Spain. The best-known poem on Lepanto in Spanish, three centuries before Chesterton's in English.

units.orig:
Cantemos al Señor que en la llanura
Venció del mar al enemigo fiero:
Tú, Dios de las batallas, tú eres diestra,
Salud y gloria nuestra.
Tú rompiste las fuerzas y la dura
Frente de Faraón, feroz guerrero:
Sus escogidos Príncipes cubrieron
Los abismos del mar, y decendieron,
Cual piedra, en el profundo; y tu ira luego
Los tragó como arista seca el fuego.
units.en: Let us sing to the Lord, who on the plain of the sea overcame the fierce enemy. You, God of battles, you are our right hand, our salvation and our glory. You broke the strength and the hard brow of Pharaoh, the fierce warrior; his chosen princes covered the depths of the sea, and went down like a stone into the deep; and then your wrath swallowed them as fire swallows dry stubble.
units.titel: Canción en alabanza de la divina majestad por la vitoria del señor don Juan
units.note: Herrera's song follows the Song of Moses after the crossing of the Red Sea (Exodus 15) and the Psalms, casting Lepanto as Israel's deliverance and the Sultan as Pharaoh. It was printed with the Relación in 1572 and became one of the most admired poems of the Spanish sixteenth century. Compare Chesterton's Lepanto of 1911 (Chest.).

units.orig:
El soberbio Tirano, confiado
En el grande aparato de sus naves,
Que de los nuestros la cerviz cativa,
Y las manos aviva
Al ministerio de su duro estado,
Derribó con los brazos suyos graves
Los cedros mas ecelsos de la cima;
Y el árbol que mas yerto se sublima,
Bebiendo agenas aguas y pisando
El mas cerrado y apartado bando.
units.en: The proud Tyrant, trusting in the great array of his ships, which holds our people's necks captive and drives their hands to the service of his hard estate, felled with his heavy arms the loftiest cedars of the summit, and the tree that rises most stiffly, drinking others' waters and trampling the most closed and distant band.
units.note: 'Our people's necks captive … their hands to the service': the Christian galley slaves at the Ottoman oars.

units.orig:
Temblaron los pequeños confundidos
Del impío furor suyo; alzó la frente
Contra tí, Señor Dios, y enfurecido
Ya contra tí se vido
Con los armados brazos extendidos
El arrogante cuello del potente.
Cercó su corazón de ardiente saña
Contra las dos Hesperias que el mar baña,
Porque en tí confiadas le resisten,
Y de armas de tu fe y amor se visten.
units.en: The small trembled, confounded by his impious fury; he raised his brow against you, Lord God, and the arrogant neck of the mighty was seen, enraged, against you with its armed arms outstretched. He girt his heart with burning rage against the two Hesperias that the sea washes, because, trusting in you, they resist him, and clothe themselves in the arms of your faith and love.
units.note: The two Hesperias: Italy and Spain, the 'western lands'.

units.orig:
Dijo aquel insolente y desdeñoso:
¿No conocen mis iras estas tierras
Y de mis padres los ilustres hechos?
¿O valieron sus pechos
Contra ellos con el Húngaro dudoso,
Y de Dalmacia y Rodas en las guerras?
¿Pudo su Dios librallos de sus manos?
¿Qué Dios salvó á los de Austria y los Germanos?
¿Por ventura podia su Dios ahora
Guardallos de mi diestra vencedora?
units.en: That insolent and scornful one said: 'Do these lands not know my wrath and the illustrious deeds of my fathers? Or did their hearts avail against them, with the wavering Hungarian, and in the wars of Dalmatia and Rhodes? Could their God free them from their hands? What God saved those of Austria and the Germans? Could their God, perhaps, keep them now from my conquering right hand?'
units.note: The Sultan's boast echoes the Assyrian's in Isaiah 36–37: 'Who are they among all the gods of these lands that have delivered their land out of mine hand?' Mohács (1526), Rhodes (1522) and the siege of Vienna (1529) are the deeds of his fathers.

units.orig:
Su Roma, temerosa y humillada,
Sus canciones en lágrimas convierte;
Ella y sus hijos mi furor esperan
Cuando vencidos mueran.
Francia está con discordia quebrantada,
Y en España amenaza horrible muerte
Quien honra de la Luna las banderas,
Y aquellas gentes en la guerra fieras
Ocupadas están en su defensa;
Y aunque no, ¿quién podría hacerme ofensa?
units.en: 'Their Rome, fearful and humbled, turns its songs to tears; she and her sons await my fury, when they die defeated. France is broken by discord, and in Spain those who honour the banners of the Moon threaten horrible death, and those peoples, fierce in war, are busy defending themselves; and even if not, who could harm me?'
units.note: France in its wars of religion; in Spain, the revolt of the Moriscos of Granada (1568–1571), 'who honour the banners of the Moon'.

units.en: 'The mighty peoples obey me, and to their harm have accepted the yoke, and give me their hand now to save themselves; and their valour is vain, for their lights grow dark as they die. Their strong ones have perished in battle; their virgins are in captivity; their glory has passed to the sceptre of my empire; from the Nile to the Euphrates and the cold Danube, all that the high sun looks on is mine.'
units.note: 'Give me their hand': Venice, which had paid tribute and kept peace with the Sultan.

units.en: You, Lord, who do not suffer your glory to be usurped by one who trusts in his greatness, prevailing in vanity and wrath: look on this proud one, who defiles your temples in his victory, and feeds the wild beasts on their bodies, and tastes his hatred in their spilt blood; and, having made them his reproach, says: 'Where is the God of these? From whom is he hiding?'
units.note: This stanza has nine lines in the 1852 reprint, checked against the page image; a line appears to be missing.

units.en: For the glory due to your name, for vengeance for your dead people, and for the groaning of the captives, turn your outstretched arm against him who now scorns to be a man and accepts the honours that are given to you; and double his punishment three and four times with strength against the enemy; and let the injury done to your name be the hard knife of his life.

units.orig:
Levantó la cabeza el poderoso,
Que tanto odio te tiene, en nuestro estrago,
Juntó el concilio; y contra nos pensaron
Los que en él se hallaron.
Venid, dijeron, y en el mar undoso
Hagamos de su sangre un grande lago;
Deshagamos á estos de la gente
Y el nombre de su Cristo juntamente;
Y dividiendo dellos los despojos,
Hártense en muerte suya nuestros ojos.
units.en: The mighty one, who hates you so, raised his head for our ruin; he gathered his council, and those who were in it took thought against us. 'Come,' they said, 'and in the billowing sea let us make a great lake of their blood; let us wipe these out from among the peoples, and the name of their Christ with them; and, dividing their spoils, let our eyes feast on their death.'
units.note: The Ottoman council in Herrera's song, after Psalm 83: 'Come, and let us cut them off from being a nation.' Compare the council in the histories: #/compare/council.

units.orig:
Vinieron de Asia y de la antigua Egito
Los Árabes y fieros Africanos,
Y los que Grecia junta mal con ellos,
Con levantados cuellos,
Con gran potencia y número infinito;
Y prometieron con sus duras manos
Encender nuestros fines y dar muerte
Con hierro á nuestra juventud mas fuerte,
Nuestros niños prender y las doncellas,
Y la gloria ofender y la luz dellas.
units.en: From Asia and ancient Egypt came the Arabs and the fierce Africans, and those whom Greece wrongly joins with them, with necks raised high, with great power and numbers without end; and they promised with their hard hands to set our borders on fire, and to put our strongest youth to the sword, to seize our children and our maidens, and to offend their glory and their light.
units.note: 'Those whom Greece wrongly joins with them': the Greek oarsmen and sailors of the Ottoman fleet.

units.orig:
Ocuparon del mar los largos senos,
En silencio y temor puesta la tierra,
Y nuestros fuertes súbitos cesaron,
Y medrosos callaron,
Hasta que á los feroces Agarenos
El Señor eligiendo nueva guerra,
Se opuso el Joven de Austria valeroso
Con el claro Español y belicoso;
Que Dios no sufre en Babilonia viva
Su querida Sion siempre cativa.
units.en: They took the wide bays of the sea, the land being put in silence and fear, and our strong ones suddenly ceased, and fell silent in fear, until, the Lord choosing a new war, the valiant Youth of Austria stood against the fierce Hagarenes, with the famous and warlike Spaniard; for God does not suffer his beloved Zion to live for ever captive in Babylon.
units.note: Hagarenes: the descendants of Hagar, a biblical name for the Muslims. Don John was twenty-four.

units.orig:
Cual león á la presa apercibido,
Esperaban los impíos confiados
A los que tú, Señor, eras escudo:
Que el corazón desnudo
De temor y de fe todo vestido,
De tu espíritu estaban confortados:
Sus manos á la guerra compusiste,
Y á sus brazos fortísimos pusiste
Como el arco acerado, y con la espada
Mostraste en su favor la diestra armada.
units.en: Like a lion ready for its prey, the confident ungodly awaited those to whom you, Lord, were a shield: who, their hearts stripped of fear and wholly clothed in faith, were comforted by your spirit. You trained their hands for war, and made their most mighty arms like a bow of steel, and with the sword you showed your armed right hand in their favour.
units.note: After Psalm 18: 'He teacheth my hands to war, so that a bow of steel is broken by mine arms.'

units.orig:
Turbáronse los grandes, los robustos
Rindiéronse temblando, y desmayaron;
Y tú pusiste, Dios, como la rueda,
Como la arista queda
Al ímpetu del viento, á estos injustos,
Que mil huyendo de uno se pasmaron:
Cual fuego abrasa selvas, y cual llama
Que en las espesas cumbres se derrama,
Tal en tu ira y tempestad seguiste,
Y su faz de ignominia confundiste.
units.en: The great were troubled; the strong surrendered trembling, and fainted; and you, God, made these unjust ones like a wheel, like the stubble left to the force of the wind, so that a thousand fled from one in terror. As fire burns the forests, and as a flame spreads over the thick summits, so you pursued them in your wrath and storm, and confounded their faces with shame.
units.note: After Psalm 83: 'O my God, make them like a wheel; as the stubble before the wind. As the fire burneth a wood …'

units.orig:
Quebrantaste al dragón fiero, cortando
Las alas de su cuerpo temerosas,
Y sus brazos terribles no vencidos:
Que con hondos gemidos
Se retira á su cueva silbos dando,
Y tiembla con sus sierpes venenosas,
Lleno de miedo torpe sus entrañas,
De tu León, temiendo las hazañas,
Que, saliendo de España, dió un rugido
Que con espanto lo dejó aturdido.
units.en: You broke the fierce dragon, cutting the fearful wings of its body and its terrible, never-conquered arms; so that with deep groans it withdraws hissing to its cave, and trembles with its poisonous serpents, its entrails full of base fear, dreading the deeds of your Lion, who, coming out of Spain, gave a roar that left it stunned with terror.
units.note: The dragon whose wings are cut: Contarini's 'the wings of the great serpent of the East were clipped' (Contarini Battle [19]). The Lion is Spain's heraldic lion and Don John.

units.orig:
Hoy los ojos se vieron humillados
Del sublime varón y su grandeza,
Y tú solo, Señor, fuiste exaltado,
Que tu dia es llegado,
Señor de los ejércitos armados,
Sobre la alta cerviz y su dureza,
Sobre derechos cedros y extendidos,
Sobre empinados montes y crecidos,
Sobre torres y muros, y las naves
De Tiro que á los tuyos fueron graves.
units.en: Today the eyes of the lofty man and his greatness were seen humbled, and you alone, Lord, were exalted, for your day has come, Lord of armed hosts, upon the high neck and its hardness, upon the straight and spreading cedars, upon the lofty and towering mountains, upon towers and walls, and the ships of Tyre that were grievous to your people.
units.note: After Isaiah 2: 'The lofty looks of man shall be humbled … for the day of the Lord of hosts shall be upon every one that is proud … upon all the cedars of Lebanon … and upon all the ships of Tarshish.'

units.orig:
Babilonia y Egito amedrentada
Del fuego y asta temblará sangrienta,
Y el humo subirá á la luz del cielo,
Y faltos de consuelo,
Con rostro oscuro y soledad turbada
Tus enemigos llorarán su afrenta.
Y tú, Grecia, concorde á la esperanza
De Egito y gloria de su confianza;
Triste, que á ellas pareces, no temiendo
A Dios, y en tu remedio no atendiendo;
units.en: Babylon and Egypt, terrified, will tremble at the bloody fire and spear, and the smoke will rise to the light of heaven, and, without comfort, with darkened faces and troubled loneliness, your enemies will weep for their shame. And you, Greece, in accord with the hope of Egypt and the glory of its trust; sad one, who are like them, not fearing God, and not seeing to your remedy;

units.orig:
¿Por qué ingrata tus hijas adornaste
En adulterio con tan impía gente,
Que deseaba profanar tus frutos,
Y con ojos enjutos
Sus odiosos pasos imitaste,
Su aborrecible vida y mal presente?
Por eso Dios se vengará en tu muerte,
Que llega á tu cerviz su diestra fuerte
La aguda espada ¿quién será que pueda
Tener su mano poderosa queda?
units.en: Why, ungrateful one, did you adorn your daughters in adultery with so impious a people, who wished to profane your fruits, and, dry-eyed, imitated their hateful steps, their abhorrent life and present evil? Therefore God will take vengeance in your death, for his strong right hand brings the sharp sword to your neck: who will there be who can hold his mighty hand still?
units.note: Herrera's reproach to the Greeks, subjects of the Sultan, many of whom rowed and sailed in his fleet.

units.orig:
Mas tú, fuerza del mar, tú, excelsa Tiro,
Que en tus naves estabas gloriosa
Y el término espantabas de la tierra,
Y si hacías guerra,
De temor la cubrías con suspiro;
¿Cómo acabaste, fiera y orgullosa?
¿Quién pensó á tu cabeza daño tanto?
Dios, para convertir tu gloria en llanto,
Y derribar tus ínclitos y fuertes,
Te hizo perecer con tantas muertes.
units.en: But you, strength of the sea, you, exalted Tyre, who were glorious in your ships and frightened the ends of the earth, and, if you made war, covered it with fear and sighing: how did you end, fierce and proud one? Who planned such harm to your head? God, to turn your glory into weeping and cast down your famous and strong ones, made you perish with so many deaths.
units.note: After Ezekiel 26–27, the lament over Tyre, city of ships: the Ottoman sea power.

units.orig:
Llorad, naves del mar, que es destruida
Toda vuestra soberbia y fortaleza.
¿Quién ya tendrá de tí lástima alguna,
Tú que sigues la Luna,
Asia adúltera en vicios sumergida?
¿Quién mostrará por tí alguna tristeza?
¿Quién rogará por tí? Que Dios entiende
Tu ira y la soberbia que le ofende;
Y tus antiguas culpas y mudanza
Han vuelto contra tí á pedir venganza.
units.en: Weep, ships of the sea, for all your pride and strength is destroyed. Who now will have any pity on you, you who follow the Moon, adulterous Asia sunk in vices? Who will show any sorrow for you? Who will pray for you? For God understands your wrath and the pride that offends him; and your ancient sins and faithlessness have turned against you to ask for vengeance.
units.note: Isaiah 23: 'Howl, ye ships of Tarshish: for your strength is laid waste.'

units.orig:
Los que vieren tus brazos quebrantados
Y de tus pinos ir el mar desnudo,
Que sus ondas turbaron y llanura;
Viendo tu muerte escura,
Dirán de tus estragos espantados:
¿Quién contra la espantosa tanto pudo?
El Señor, que mostró su fuerte mano
Por la fe de su Príncipe cristiano,
Y por el nombre santo de su gloria
A España le concede esta vitoria.
units.en: Those who see your arms broken, and the sea going bare of your pines, which troubled its waves and its plain, seeing your dark death, will say, astonished at your ruin: 'Who could do so much against the fearsome one?' The Lord, who showed his strong hand for the faith of his Christian Prince, and for the holy name of his glory grants this victory to Spain.
units.note: 'To Spain': the song gives the victory to Spain alone. Contarini's history gives it to God and the League's three generals, and ends in Venice (Contarini Reckoning [7]).

units.orig:
Bendita, Señor, sea tu grandeza,
Que después de los daños padecidos,
Después de nuestras culpas y castigo,
Rompiste al enemigo
De la antigua soberbia la dureza.
Adórente, Señor, tus escogidos;
Confiese cuanto cerca el ancho cielo
Tu nombre, ó nuestro Dios, nuestro consuelo;
Y la cerviz rebelde condenada
Padezca en bravas llamas abrasada.

A tí solo la gloria
Por siglos de los siglos, á tí damos
La honra y humillados te adoramos.
units.en:
Blessed, Lord, be your greatness, who, after the harm we suffered, after our sins and punishment, broke the hardness of the enemy's ancient pride. Let your chosen ones adore you, Lord; let all that the wide heaven encircles confess your name, O our God, our comfort; and let the rebellious, condemned neck suffer, burned in fierce flames.

To you alone the glory for ever and ever; to you we give the honour, and humbled we adore you.
units.note: The closing three lines are the envoi (commiato) of the canción.
